zh:
【丧服第十一】

丧服，斩衰裳，苴絰杖，绞带，冠绳缨，菅屦者。诸侯为天子，君，父为长子，为人后者。妻为夫，妾为君，女子子在室为父，布总，箭笄，髽，衰，三年。子嫁，反在父之室，为父三年。公士、大夫之众臣，为其君布带、绳屦。
疏衰裳齐，牡麻絰，冠布缨，削杖，布带，疏屦三年者，父卒则为母，继母如母，慈母如母，母为长子。
疏衰裳齐，牡麻絰，冠布缨，削杖，布带，疏屦，期者，父在为母，妻，出妻之子为母。出妻之子为父后者则为出母无服。父卒，继母嫁，从，为之服，报。
不杖，麻屦者。祖父母，世父母，叔父母；大夫之适子为妻，昆弟；为众子，昆弟之子；大夫之庶子为适昆弟适孙。为人后者，为其父母，报。女子子适人者为其父母、昆弟之为父后者，继父同居者，为夫之君。姑、姊妹、女子子适人无主者，姑、姊妹报。为君之父、母、妻、长子、祖父母。妾为女君。妇为舅姑，夫之昆弟之子。公妾、大夫之妾为其子。女子子为祖父母。大夫之子为世父母、叔父母、子、昆弟、昆弟之子，姑、姊妹、女子子无主者，为大夫命妇者，唯子不报。大夫为祖父母、适孙为士者。公妾以及士妾为其父母。
疏衰裳齐，牡麻絰，无受者。寄公为所寓，丈夫、妇人为宗子、宗子之母、妻，为旧君、君之母、妻，庶人为国君；大夫在外，其妻、长子为旧国君；继父不同居者，曾祖父母，大夫为宗子，旧君。曾祖父母为士者如众人，女子子嫁者、未嫁者为曾祖父母。
大功布衰裳，牡麻絰，无受者：子、女子子之长殇、中殇，叔父之长殇、中殇，姑、姊妹之长殇、中殇，昆弟之长殇、中殇，夫之昆弟之子、女子子之长殇、中殇，适孙之长殇、中殇，大夫之庶子为适昆弟子之长殇、中殇，公子之长殇、中殇，大夫为适子之长殇、中殇。其长殇皆九月，缨絰；其中殇，七月，不缨絰。
大功布衰裳，牡麻絰缨，布带，三月。受以小功衰，即葛，九月者：姑、姊妹、女子子适人者，从父昆弟；为人后者为其昆弟，庶孙；适妇，女子子适人者为众昆弟；侄丈夫妇人，报。夫之祖父母、世父母、叔父母，大夫为世父母、叔父母、子、昆弟、昆弟之子为士者；公之庶昆弟、大夫之庶子为母、妻、昆弟，皆为其从父昆弟之为大夫者；为夫之昆弟之妇人子适人者；大夫之妾为君之庶子；女子子嫁者、未嫁者，为世父母、叔父母、姑、姊妹，大夫、大夫之妻、大夫之子、公之昆弟为姑、姊妹、女子子嫁于大夫者，君为姑、姊妹、女子子嫁于国君者。
繐衰裳，牡麻絰，既葬除之者。诸侯之大夫为天子。
……
en:
【Mourning Apparel, Part 11】

For mourning attire: the coarse hempen sackcloth for the upper and lower garments, the hempen cord for the mourning staff, the girdle of twisted hemp, the cap with hempen cord, and the shoes of rushes—these are worn: by the feudal lords for the Son of Heaven; by the ruler; by a father for his eldest son, and for one who continues the family line; by a wife for her husband; by a concubine for her lord; by an unmarried daughter for her father, with her hair bound in a cloth, wearing a hairpin of arrow bamboo, and with her hair in a mourning knot, in sackcloth—for three years. A daughter who has married but returns to her father's house mourns for her father for three years. The many servants of a nobleman or a great officer wear for their lord a hempen girdle and shoes of rushes.
For the mourning of coarse hempen sackcloth with even edges, with the hempen cord for the mourning staff, the cap with hempen cord, the staff of cut wood, the hempen girdle, and the shoes of coarse hemp—for three years: when the father is deceased, then for the mother; for a stepmother as for a mother; for a foster mother as for a mother; and by a mother for her eldest son.
For the mourning of coarse hempen sackcloth with even edges, with the hempen cord for the mourning staff, the cap with hempen cord, the staff of cut wood, the hempen girdle, and the shoes of coarse hemp—for one year: when the father is living, for the mother; for a wife; by the son of a divorced woman for his mother. The son of a divorced woman who continues the father's line does not wear mourning for his divorced mother. When the father is deceased and the stepmother remarries, if one follows her, one wears mourning for her, and she reciprocates.
For those who do not use the staff, with shoes of hemp: for grandparents, for uncles and aunts (the elder and younger brothers of the father and their wives); by the legitimate son of a great officer for his wife; for brothers; for younger sons and for the sons of brothers; by the sons of a great officer's concubines for their legitimate elder brothers and legitimate grandsons. For one who continues another's line, for his own parents—and they reciprocate. For a married daughter for her parents and for her brothers who continue the father's line; for a stepfather with whom one resides; for the lord's ruler. For aunts, sisters, and daughters who have married and have no one to preside over their sacrifices—and the aunts and sisters reciprocate. For the ruler's father, mother, wife, eldest son, and grandparents. By a concubine for the legitimate wife. By a wife for her father-in-law and mother-in-law, and for the sons of her husband's brothers. By the concubines of a duke or a great officer for their own sons. By a daughter for her grandparents. By the son of a great officer for his uncles and aunts, for his sons, brothers, and the sons of his brothers, and for aunts, sisters, and daughters who have no one to preside over their sacrifices—when these are wives of great officers who have received the mandate; only the son does not reciprocate. By a great officer for his grandparents, and for a legitimate grandson who is a knight. By the concubines of a duke and the concubines of a knight for their own parents.
For the mourning of coarse hempen sackcloth with even edges, with the hempen cord for the mourning staff, without the subsequent change of mourning garments: by a refugee lord for the lord who gives him shelter; by men and women for the clan head, for the mother and wife of the clan head; for a former ruler, and for the mother and wife of a former ruler; by common people for the ruler of the state; when a great officer is abroad, by his wife and eldest son for the former ruler of the state; for a stepfather with whom one does not reside; for great-grandparents; by a great officer for the clan head and for a former ruler. For great-grandparents who are knights, as for the common people; by daughters, whether married or unmarried, for their great-grandparents.
For the mourning of the great merit cloth of sackcloth, with the hempen cord for the mourning staff, without the subsequent change of mourning garments: for the untimely death (in youth or middle age) of sons and daughters; for the untimely death of uncles (younger brothers of the father); for the untimely death of aunts and sisters; for the untimely death of brothers; for the untimely death of the sons and daughters of a husband's brothers; for the untimely death of a legitimate grandson; by the sons of a great officer's concubines for the untimely death of the sons of their legitimate brothers; for the untimely death of the sons of a duke or a great officer; by a great officer for the untimely death of his legitimate son. All these untimely deaths in youth are mourned for nine months, with the hempen cord with tassels; those in middle age are mourned for seven months, without the tasseled cord.
For the mourning of the great merit cloth of sackcloth, with the hempen cord with tassels for the mourning staff, the hempen girdle, for three months. Then changing to the lesser merit sackcloth, and then to the hempen cloth, for nine months: for aunts, sisters, and daughters who have married; for the sons of paternal cousins; by one who continues another's line for his brothers; for grandsons by concubines; for the legitimate daughter-in-law; by a married daughter for her many brothers; for nephews and nieces, and they reciprocate. For the grandparents, uncles, and aunts of a husband; by a great officer for his uncles and aunts, for his sons, brothers, and the sons of his brothers who are knights; by the younger brothers of a duke and the sons of a great officer's concubines for their mothers, wives, and brothers—all these for their paternal cousins who are great officers; for the married daughters of a husband's brothers; by the concubine of a great officer for the sons of her lord by his concubines; by daughters, whether married or unmarried, for their uncles and aunts, and for their aunts and sisters; by a great officer, the wife of a great officer, the son of a great officer, and the brothers of a duke for aunts, sisters, and daughters married to great officers; by a ruler for aunts, sisters, and daughters married to rulers of states.
For the mourning of the fine hempen sackcloth, with the hempen cord for the mourning staff, to be removed after the burial: by the great officers of the feudal lords for the Son of Heaven.

zh:
海气生重雾，雾幻结楼台。忽闻有宝船，纵横南北冥。得之驾长风，直赴蓬莱宴。东来日升处，高卧扶桑间。
青州海上，传说纷纭。有传八仙欲渡海，掷法器立波。有舟子欲相随，奈何无舟，欲寻宝船。宝船者，首雕胖鱼，身耀龙鳞，驾之可御风乘浪，随八仙东游，至蓬莱仙山。据说啊，那仙山在虚无缥缈间，山上一天，人间一年！
沿海径一带的渔民常给孩子讲八仙的传说，只是在孩童讲来，这故事怎么和别人不太一样？没有宝船——骑羊也行！
en:
"Sea mist rises thick, conjuring towering pavilions. A fabled treasure ship sails the northern and southern seas. Ride it on the great winds to Penglai, then east to where the sun rises, to rest among the sacred branches."

The seas off Qingzhou are full of legend. One tale says that when the Eight Immortals set out to cross the sea, a boatman wished to follow but had no boat of his own, so he went searching for a treasure ship. Its prow was carved like a plump fish, its hull shone with dragon scales, and aboard it one could ride the wind and waves east with the Eight Immortals to Mount Penglai. They say that immortal mountain lies in a realm beyond reach, where one day on the mountain is a whole year in the mortal world.
Fisherfolk along the Cliffside Path often tell children stories of the Eight Immortals. But when children tell the story back, it never comes out quite the same. No treasure ship? Then riding a goat will do!

幻术泡影，大者如瓮，小者如斗，凝而不散，又有五色流转其中，晃若虹霓，而中空莹澈，可容人入，宛坐琉璃世界中。每于市肆间施此技，观者如堵。
幻师曰：“浮生扰扰，何异于梦幻泡影？然则梦幻泡影，亦足乐耳。”

en:
It is said that in the Tang dynasty, there lived an illusionist whose name has been lost to time, and who often wandered among the markets and stalls. One day, he chanced upon a temple gate, where a woman was chanting sutras. When she reached the verse, "All things are as a dream within a bubble, fleeting as the morning dew or the thunder. Thus, we should contemplate so." The illusionist was suddenly enlightened. And so he devised a technique, one which he named Phantom Bubble.
The largest bubbles conjured by this illusion are as broad as an urn, the smallest as small as a peck-measure. They held their form without dispersing, and within them swirled five colors, shimmering like a rainbow. Their hollow centers remained clear and translucent, large enough to hold a person, the world within was that of a glazed crystal. Whenever he performed this art amid the markets, onlookers would gather in crowds.
The illusionist once said, "Life is fleeting, no more than a dream in a bubble. Yet even dreams and bubbles have their joys."
Later, this technique spread to the central land. It brought great joy to the children, and they would spend a whole day playing and chasing the bubbles.
A tale of the fleeting past, such a wondrous thing indeed.

In ancient times, there was a rare incense known as "Harmony Incense." When burned in a Boshan censer, it conjured visions of mountain peaks veiled by drifting clouds.

This incense was valued above gold. Few realize, however, that it can only be found within the censer carried by a Boshan Censer Camel.

Throughout its life, the camel nurtures a single piece of this precious incense. When it rests, delicate wisps of smoke rise from its back, shimmering in the light. The incense is fully formed only when the camel ages naturally.

zh:
杨帆到耕读村那天，带了三样东西。一包袱书，一罐腌咸菜，一个空本子。
本子是他在文津馆时就备下的。同窗问他带空本子干啥，他说记村里的事。同窗说，你是村官，又不是史官，记啥？他没接话。本子揣进包袱里，贴着心口那侧。
他是真想做点事。
在文津馆读书时，先生讲《孟子》，讲到“民为贵”，他坐在底下听着，心里像被什么东西撞了一下。后来考吏员，他填了耕读村。同窗说那地方偏，路远，你去那儿图啥。他说，总得有人去。
到村里的头一天安顿下，他没歇。挨家挨户走，走到天黑，本子上记了十几页。谁家老人腿脚不好，谁家屋顶漏雨，谁家孩子到了年纪还没进学，谁家葱地今年遭了虫。一条一条，字挤得密密麻麻。
后来村里人发现，这个年轻村官的本子上，圈越来越多。圈上的意思是待办。办完了，圈就涂掉，旁边写上办了什么事，字小小的，挤在边角上。
他走路还有个毛病，嘴里老念叨。有回一头撞在老树上，额头起了个包。孙大爷在树底下乘凉，说帆子啊，树又没动。他捂着额头说，想事呢。
孙大爷问他，你这天天跑东家跑西家，图啥。
帆子想了想，最后说，总得对得起乡亲。
孙大爷没再问。抽了口烟，说额头那个包，回去拿凉水敷敷。
他应了一声，走了。孙大爷看着他的背影，嘟囔了一句。
“傻小子。”
杨帆没听见。他在想王奶奶家的水缸明天还得挑，张婶家的鸡得再去看一趟，村东头那截路下雨就泞，得想法子。
本子揣在怀里，贴着心口那侧。
一页一页，越记越厚。
en:
When Yang Fan arrived in Sageplow Stead, he brought exactly three things with him: a wrapped bundle of books, a jar of pickled vegetables, and a blank notebook.
He'd picked up the notebook back when he was studying at the Inkbound Order. When a classmate asked what it was for, Yang Fan simply said he planned to keep a record of village affairs. "You're going to be a village officer, not an imperial historian," the classmate scoffed. "What could you possibly need to write down?" Yang Fan didn't answer. He just tucked the notebook into his satchel, keeping it close against his chest.
He truly wanted to do some good.
Back at the Inkbound Order, a master had once given a lecture on the philosophy of Mencius. When the master spoke the words, "The people come first," Yang Fan felt it strike a chord deep in his chest. Later, when it came time to submit his civil service placement, he specifically asked for Sageplow Stead. His peers warned him that the region was a remote, grueling backwater. They couldn't understand what he hoped to gain by going out there. "Someone has to go," he replied.
He didn't take a single moment to rest on his first day. Instead, he walked from door to door until the sun went down. By nightfall, he had filled over a dozen pages with tiny, dense handwriting. He noted which elders had bad knees, whose roofs leaked in the rain, whose kids were old enough for school but weren't attending, and whose leek crops were being eaten by pests.
Before long, the villagers noticed that the young official's notebook was filling up with hand-drawn circles. A circle meant a job to be done. Once he handled it, he would cross the circle out and scribble a quick note in the margins explaining how he'd fixed it.
Yang Fan had a terrible habit of muttering to himself as he walked. Once, entirely lost in thought, he walked face-first into an old tree, raising a nasty lump on his forehead. Old Man Sun, who was resting in the shade nearby, just chuckled. "Careful, Fan. That tree isn't going to jump out of your way." Rubbing his head, Yang Fan sheepishly admitted his mind was elsewhere.
"You run yourself ragged from one end of this village to the other every single day," Old Man Sun said, taking a slow drag from his pipe. "What are you even after?"
Yang Fan thought about it for a moment. "I just want to do right by the folks here."
Old Man Sun didn't press him. He just exhaled a puff of smoke. "Go put some cold water on that lump."
As Yang Fan nodded and walked away, the old man watched him go and muttered, "Silly boy."
Yang Fan didn't hear him. His mind was already racing ahead to tomorrow: he needed to fetch water for Granny Wang, check on Aunt Zhang's chickens one more time, and figure out how to pave the east road before the rains turned it to mud.
The notebook remained safely tucked inside his robes, resting right over his heart.
Page by page, it was growing thicker.

zh:
长风万里，终度玉门。你来到了那座巍峨的城关之下。此刻，它已不是难以越过的雄关天堑，而是春风西行的驿站。在旌旗飘扬的风沙里，你仿佛又一次看到了那位白头将军，正站在城墙之上，远眺东方。他眼里所见，心中所念，口中所说的皆为一句话：长安，如今可好？你踌躇半晌，开口道……
⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛⬛
听闻你的回答，将军颔首沉吟，眼中似有热泪。“长安……是个很好，很好的地方。”将军浑厚苍凉的嗓音里带着怀念，也带着慨然。满城少年变白发，手中的锋镞依然，归唐之心依然。城中传来阵阵鼓声，似有千军万马列阵。你听不清他们口中呼喊的名字，但你知道，那是千万乡音汇成的两个字——长安。
en:
The endless winds travel thousands of miles, finally passing through Jade Gate Pass. You arrive beneath that towering fortress. It is no longer an impassable stronghold, but a waystation for the spring breeze journeying west. In the windblown sand, with banners snapping overhead, you seem to glimpse the white-haired general once more, standing atop the wall and gazing east. What he sees in his eyes, holds in his heart, and speaks on his lips all resolve into a single refrain: "How fares Chang'an now?" You hesitate for a long while and say...

Hearing your answer, the general nods in silent thought, tears seemingly welling in his eyes. "Chang'an... is a very, very fine place." The general's deep and desolate voice carries a sense of nostalgia, as well as a profound sorrow. The youths of the city have turned white-haired, yet the weapons in their hands remain sharp, as does their resolve to return to the Tang. From within the city comes the rolling beat of drums, as if an army of thousands were falling into formation. You cannot clearly hear the name they cry, but you know it is a single name formed by thousands of homesick voices: Chang'an.

她从小就知道，自己不是个喵才。
她只喜欢摸鱼抓老鼠，喜欢风吹麦田，喜欢这花花的人间。

en:
Florid, Florid, always chasing the wonders of the human world. 
She and her brother Moonbeam came out from Yiqiu Gate. Her brother hurried to the Imperial Garden, while she walked toward the fields and hills. 
Even as a kitten, she knew that she wasn't born to be great. 
She just liked catching fish, chasing mice. Liked the wind through the wheat fields. And the colors of this messy, lovely world. 
In spring planting and autumn harvest, when people bustle with work, Florid rolls in piles of rice. 
That is her greatest joy in life.

en: Oat Meal, a humble yet time-honored dish, traces its origins back to the Han Dynasty. In The Rapid Primer by Shi You of the Western Han, there is a line: "Flatbreads, wheatmeal rice, and sweet bean soup." Centuries later, the poet Lu You wrote: "A clay pot of wheatmeal shared with the old neighbor," and "In festive times, every household is filled with its rich aroma." By the Northern Song period, wheatmeal rice had become a daily staple for the people. Sprinkled with tender acacia buds and wild chives, the green and yellow hues made it visually enticing. Though its rough texture—thanks to the wheat bran—left a lasting impression, the bran helped stave off hunger, and the wild greens provided essential nutrition. For those living near the Forsaken Quarter, it was a rare and treasured meal.

【宫室·三】

【寺】

灵隐寺
宋之问
鹫岭郁岧峣，龙宫锁寂寥。
楼观沧海日，门对浙江潮。
桂子月中落，天香云外飘。

霜薄花更发，冰轻叶未凋。

待入天台路，看余度石桥。

题破山寺后禅院

清晨入古寺，初日照高林。
竹径通幽处，禅房花木深。
山光悦鸟性，潭影空人心。
万籁此俱寂，惟闻钟磬音。

净土堂
柳宗元
结习自无始，沦溺穷苦源。
流形及兹世，始悟三空门。
华堂开净域，图像焕且繁。
清冷焚众香，微妙歌法言。
稽首愧导师，超遥谢尘昏。
en:
【Palaces and Halls · Three】

【Temples】

Lingyin Temple
Song Zhiwen
The Vulture Peak towers high and steep, the Dragon Palace locked in deep silence.
From its towers, one watches the sun rise over the sea; its gates face the tidal bore of the Zhejiang River.
Cassia seeds fall from the moon, celestial fragrance drifts beyond the clouds.
Climbing the pagoda afar by grasping vines, fetching distant spring water by hollowing wood.
Frost is light, yet flowers bloom more; ice is thin, leaves have not yet withered.
From youth, I admired distant wonders; seeking and facing them washes away worldly clamor.
Awaiting the path to Tiantai Mountain, watch me cross the stone bridge.

In the Rear Meditation Hall of the Broken Hill Temple
Chang Jian
At dawn I enter the ancient temple, the first sun shines on the tall woods.
A bamboo path leads to a secluded place, the meditation hall deep amidst flowers and trees.
Mountain scenery delights the nature of birds, pond reflections empty the human heart.
All sounds here are utterly silent, only the chime of bells is heard.

Hall of the Pure Land
Liu Zongyuan
Habitual tendencies have no beginning, drowning in the source of suffering.
Flowing through forms until this world, I first awaken to the Three Gates of Emptiness.
The splendid hall opens the pure realm, its images radiant and abundant.
Cool and clear, burning all incense, subtle and wondrous, singing the Dharma words.
I bow my head, ashamed before the guiding teacher, transcending afar, bidding farewell to the dusty gloom.

en:
Heron's eyesight had grown dim, and Gasping Cliff was dark even on a good day. Whenever she dropped something, she could never seem to find it again.
Today it was a hairpin, and not just any hairpin. It was the prize she had won for taking first place in the Young Prodigy Contest as a child, an egret hairpin carved by the Grandmaster himself. She used to wear it every day, back when she still had sharp eyes that could read people and judge things at a glance.
She searched and searched, but it was nowhere to be found. In the end she thought, bitterly, "If it's gone, it's gone. Same as my sight."
Just as she was about to give up, a newly admitted junior disciple came over, grinning, and handed it back to her.
"It was on the rock right behind you. If you'd just turned around, you'd have seen it."

zh:
“周红线，捉纸鸢去呀！”
纸鸢断线的时候，神仙渡的孩子们都急了，眼见着纸鸢越飞越远，落在了远远山坡的树上。
红线弄断了线，咬着嘴巴，就往那里跑。
“你们等着，我把纸鸢捉回来。”

红线一路向着纸鸢的方向跑，暮色渐渐重起来。等她艰难地爬到树上，拿到那只纸鸢的时候，日头彻底沉下去了。
从高处看孩子们的方向，早已无人了，都已被各自的娘亲领回家吃饭。
算算时候……爹爹应该还在酒厂、没有下工吧。
红线抓着纸鸢，生怕又被风吹掉了。但这树好高，方才还不觉得，如今回过味来、又抓着纸鸢，倒真的不敢下去了。
夜色越来越浓，凉风露重，红线在没有人知道的高处，看着底下一家家的灯笼都亮起来。
红线刻意睁大眼睛，让风把眼眶吹得干干的。她可是要做女侠的人，这点小事才没有什么的！
就算谁也不知道她在这儿，就算没有人来找她，就算一、一个人在树上过一晚，也不会怕的。
她周红线，不怕黑，也不怕一个人！

不知道过了多久，红线数了三遍，神仙渡晚上的灯笼，一共有两百六十八盏。
又冷又饿，她在寒风中缩成小小的一团，迷迷糊糊地想，这下可真的要在树上过一晚上了……
恍惚间，她看见远处有一盏小灯笼，似乎是这山间唯一的光，一跳一跳地，向她跳来了。
“红线、红线！”
灯笼越来越近了，还会说话。
“红线、红线！”
……咦？
灯笼照出一张世上顶好顶温柔的脸，担忧又关切地仰头看她。
……这是梦吗？红线撒开手，纸鸢轻轻飘下，被底下的人接得稳稳当当。
“老大！”
她终于喊出声，带着哭腔。
en:
"Ruby, go catch the kite!"
When the string broke, all the children at Heaven's Pier panicked as they watched the kite drift further away, landing in a distant hillside tree.
Ruby had broken the string. Biting her lip, she ran toward it.
"Wait here! I'll fetch it back."

She raced toward the kite as twilight deepened. By the time she had climbed the tree and retrieved it, the sun had completely set.
Looking down toward where the children had been, she saw no one—all had been taken home for dinner by their mothers.
By now... her father should still be working at the winery, not yet finished for the day.
Ruby clutched the kite tightly, afraid the wind might take it again. But the tree was so tall—climbing up hadn't seemed difficult, but now, holding the kite, she dared not descend.
The night grew thicker, the air turned cold with dew, and Ruby sat alone in her lofty perch, watching as lanterns lit up one household after another below.
She deliberately widened her eyes, letting the wind dry them completely. She was going to be a heroine someday—this was nothing!
Even if nobody knew she was here, even if no one came looking, even if she had to... had to spend the night in this tree alone, she wouldn't be afraid.
She, Zhou Ruby, feared neither darkness nor solitude!

After what seemed an eternity, Ruby had counted the evening lanterns of Heaven's Pier three times: two hundred and sixty-eight in total.
Cold and hungry, she curled into a tiny ball against the biting wind, drowsily thinking that she really would spend the night in this tree after all...
In her daze, she spotted a small lantern in the distance, seemingly the only light in these hills, bobbing closer and closer toward her.
"Ruby! Ruby!"
The lantern approached, somehow speaking.
"Ruby!"
...Hmm?
The lantern illuminated the kindest, gentlest face in the world, looking up at her with worry and care.
...Was this a dream? Ruby let go, and the kite floated down, caught firmly by the person below.
"It's you!"
She finally called out, her voice breaking with tears.

zh:

云别秋不想管。行走江湖，不管闲事才是保命要诀。
她看着那琴师吃饱喝足了，在身上摸了一会儿，什么都没摸到，脸腾地一下红了起来。
眼瞧着小二就来收账，云别秋念头一转，手里握着银子站起来，又打算救这文弱家伙一把。
没想到他推开了云别秋的手，抱着琴就上了酒馆一张桌子。
她破天荒地在一家酒馆里待了三天。琴师的曲子日日准时响起，酒馆里头的杀伐之气登时稀薄许多。
原来还有这种……文明的解决方式吗？
云别秋看了看手中的剑，再看了看他的琴。在他抱琴同酒馆老板告别时，云别秋提剑跟上了他。
琴师转身同她作揖。云别秋慌了神色，手忙脚乱地回了个抱拳。
云别秋破天荒头一回想，要是当年学琴的时候，再认真一点就好了……
en:
In a tavern, a hand slipped quietly toward a diner's coin pouch.
Yun Bieqiu looked away. In the Jianghu, minding your own business was how you stayed alive.
Then she saw the victim, a thin, scholarly Guqin player, finish his meal and fumble through his robes, finding nothing. Color rushed to his face.
The waiter was already on his way. Yun Bieqiu hesitated, then rose with a piece of silver in hand. Fine. She'd save this frail musician one more time.
Before she could, he pushed her hand aside, hugged his Guqin to his chest, and climbed straight onto a table in the center of the tavern.
She stayed there for three days. Each day, the Guqin player performed on time. And with every melody, the sharp, violent air of the tavern thinned, little by little.
So... this was another way to settle things?
Yun Bieqiu glanced at the sword in her hand, then at the Guqin in his arms. When he finally packed up and bowed farewell to the innkeeper, she followed, with a blade at her side.
The Guqin player turned and greeted her with a proper salute. Yun Bieqiu froze, then fumbled an awkward return.
For the first time, a thought she'd never allowed herself crossed her mind, "If only I'd practiced the Guqin more seriously back then..."
In this world, things are always tough!

zh: 宋代对浮水葫芦的称呼，又称“要舟”、“腰船”。取成熟大葫芦，去瓤晾干，以竹篾或藤条编网套护，系于腰间或挟于腋下，即可借浮力渡水。葫芦中空可存放衣物干粮，加盖密封则不惧风浪。因其轻便实用，宋代沿海渔民常佩之防溺。
en: During the Song dynasty, people used hollowed-out gourds as personal flotation devices. To make one, a large, mature gourd was hollowed out, dried, and wrapped in a woven bamboo or rattan net. Tied around the waist or tucked under the arm, it allowed a person to safely cross the water. The hollow center could even hold clothes and dry food. Once the gourd was sealed tightly, the contents stayed perfectly dry, regardless of wind and waves. Since it was so light and practical, fishermen in the Song dynasty often wore them to prevent drowning.

年逾古稀之后，人的记性便越来越差了。
一日午休过后，张议潮倏然自梦中醒来，像是想起了什么似的，对着外间喊道：小石头，去看看那个“赶饭时”的禄伯走到哪儿了？
外间并无他人，只有自幼跟随他的老仆石叟，如今亦过了花甲之年，偶然听到这久违的称呼，登时吓了一跳——小石头是他少年时的诨名，已经三十多年没人叫过了。
石叟上前帮助年迈的张议潮更衣，无奈叹道：将军，你睡糊涂了，这是梦到了多少年前的事？……如今是咸通十年，我们在长安，你的禄伯在河西呢。
是了……禄伯在河西呢。张议潮想起来了，前日禄伯还托人送了信来，说是凉州、甘州、沙洲、肃州今岁皆是丰年，归义军又击退了乌护，打了胜仗，让他放心……
张议潮喃喃道：来长安前，我托禄伯佑百姓温饱，护边陲太平，他果然都做到了……
石叟帮他穿好了衣服，又上前帮他穿鞋，不住地絮叨：都说你们叔侄情逾父子，故以九边功业授之……可要我说，将军一点也不疼小张将军，若是真疼他，怎会舍得把他送到那高处不胜寒的地方？
张议潮愣怔了半天，竟一句话也答不出来。
石叟叹了口气，不再言语，为他焚了安神的香，把他扶起到檐边坐下。少时射天狼、挽天河的将军，如今只剩下一把犹带铜声的瘦骨。
梦里冰河铁马，梦醒后却只能闲坐庭前，消此永昼。
张议潮居长安三载，髀肉皆销，牙齿松落，白头不胜簪。
黄金为网，囿龙战之躯，百战勋业尽遗尘。
及大限至时，张议潮诸事皆忘：忘当年鏖战，忘复归大唐，忘神武军中受印……还能记得的，便只剩下一些无关紧要的小事。
比如，他其实与石叟一样，惟愿禄伯面临大事时多加珍重自身，无病无灾到公卿……至于禄伯所面临的“大事”到底是什么，他倒有些想不起来了。
又比如，禄伯十岁那年，自己征战沙洲得胜归来，约悟真法师赴雪岭古寺斋供，喜欢“赶饭时”的禄伯听了之后，非要缠着他一起去。
张议潮那时尚年轻，加之常年习武，走在陡峭的雪山上如履平地，不多时便把十岁的侄子远远甩在了身后。他走到山顶时，不放心地回头看向山下——禄伯正踏着他之前踩出的脚印，嚅息而上。
“要帮忙吗？”
“不要！叔父能爬上来，我也可以！”
张议潮哈哈大笑，他倚着一棵几可参天的枯树，决定停下来等一等这要强的小鬼。
暖冬晴好，不远处的古刹间已升起袅袅炊烟。
想必悟真今日为他们准备的斋饭是绵软的佛豆与碧绿的冬葵。
en:
Memory becomes a fickle thing once a man passes seventy. 
One afternoon, just after a nap, Zhang Yichao wakes with a jolt as though suddenly remembering something important. He calls out toward the outer room, "Little Stone, go and see where Huaishen has gotten to. He never misses a meal." 
No one is out there but his longtime attendant, Elder Stone, already past sixty himself. Hearing that childhood name "Little Stone," a name no one has used for him in over thirty years, Elder Stone is startled. 
He steps forward to help the elderly Zhang Yichao dress, and sighs, "General, you're still half-dreaming. Just how many years back did you wander this time? It's the tenth year of Xiantong. We're in Chang'an. And Huaishen is far away in Hexi." 
Ah, that's right… Huaishen is in Hexi. Zhang Yichao then recalls that just days ago, a letter arrived from him, bearing good news: Liangzhou, Ganzhou, Shazhou, and Suzhou have seen a fine harvest this year, and the Guiyi Army has driven back the Oghuz tribes, victories all along the frontier. Reassuring words. 
He murmurs, "Before I left for the capital, I asked him to keep the people fed and the borders quiet. And he hasn't let me down." 
Elder Stone finishes dressing him, helps him into his shoes, and chatters on as he works. "They say you two are like father and son, and that's why you gave him command of the frontier. But if you ask me, you've no heart for the young General Zhang. If you truly cared, you'd never have left him in a place so high and so cold." 
For a long moment, Zhang Yichao sits in stunned silence. 
Elder Stone sighs deeply and says no more. He lights some incense to settle his master's mind, and then helps him to a seat beneath the eaves. The once mighty general is now just a frail, gaunt figure, though if you listen closely, his bones still seem to ring faintly with the echo of bronze. 
In dreams, iron-clad hooves thunder across frozen rivers. In waking, he sits idle in the courtyard, letting the endless daylight slip away. 
Three years in the capital, and the muscle has withered from his thighs; his teeth loosen, and his white hair grows too sparse to hold a jade pin. 
A gilded net now traps a body forged for war. A lifetime of glory, left to settle in the dust. 
As his final hour nears, memories slip away: the roar of battle, the return to the Great Tang... all forgotten. The only things that remain are trivial, ordinary memories. 
Elder Shi, for instance. And the simple wish that Huaishen would take care when the storm breaks, living a life free of illness and strife and rising to the highest ranks... Yet Zhang can no longer recall that very "storm" facing Huaishen. 
Then there is this: when Huaishen was ten years old, Zhang Yichao had returned victorious from a campaign in Shazhou and invited the monk Wuzhen to share a vegetarian meal at the ancient temple on the snowy mountain. Huaishen, who never missed a chance to follow his uncle to a meal, had insisted on tagging along. 
Back then, Zhang Yichao was still young and strong, hardened by years of martial training. Climbing the steep, snow-covered peak was nothing to him, and he soon left his ten-year-old nephew far behind. When he reached the summit, he turned back anxiously, and there was Huaishen, carefully placing his feet in the footprints Zhang had left, climbing steadily upward. 
"Need a hand?" 
"No! If you can make it, so can I!" 
Zhang Yichao laughed, a great booming sound. He leaned against a towering dead tree and decided to wait for that stubborn little boy. 
A fine, warm winter's day. Wisps of cooking smoke rose from the ancient temple nearby. 
Surely, Wuzhen had already prepared soft broad beans and tender winter okra for their meal today.

zh:
从寒香寻手里接过离人泪的那一刻，天不收敏锐捕捉到了惊鸿影若有若无的味道。
他知道，她的香又要用完了。
翩若惊鸿，宛若游龙。这是曹子建写给洛神的诗，也是天不收送给洛神的礼物，他最得意的作品。

乱世之中，沉水香已价过千金。
好在，活人医馆里还有些扶林国的行货。这味药材珍贵，天不收不允许任何人染指。
沉水香浓郁厚重，沾衣不散，缠绵氤氲，又是一方辟邪安神的良药。
天不收小心地用柳叶刀刮取了些粉末。看了看瓷碗中薄薄的一层粉末，天不收咬咬牙，又补上两刀。
天不收总是把最好的留给寒香寻，把最坏的留给自己。

不羡仙宣布，寒娘子外出寻时鲜，不羡仙照常营业。
而清河某处荒野，几个契丹斥候被无声无息毒杀，不知何人所为。
据说，那些中毒之人脏腑都烂成了粥。连秃鹰都不愿靠近。
没有人知道，寒香寻在弱水身受重伤，此时正躺在井下休养。

寒香寻醒来当晚，便约天不收在枯井下会面。
“你不该这样意气用事。”
“你怀疑我？我是大夫，怎么能杀人。”面对寒香寻微微责怪的眼神，天不收一脸委屈，藏不住的笑意却在眼底流转。
他明白，这点演技在寒香寻面前一戳即破。
“没经验，下手重了些。”待寒香寻离去，天不收轻轻摇了摇头。
为了她的平安，自己这双手沾了血又何妨。
除掉那些见过寒香寻的人，她才能放心。何况，她伤得那么重。

几味香方钻入鼻孔，让天不收的思绪回到当下。配好新香，天不收微微一笑。
天不收走出寒香寻房间的时候， 更漏又开始催着夜色。
温柔的清风月色洒落在小房间里。寒香寻的铜镜旁，放着崭新的瓷瓶。
en:
When Unfated Tian took Parting Tears from Han Xiangxun's hands, he caught the faintest trace of Fleeting Glimpse of Beauty lingering on her.
Her perfume was running out again.
"Graceful as a startled swan, supple as a wandering dragon." Those were the words Cao Zhi had written for the Water Lady, the same ones Unfated Tian had borrowed for his masterpiece, the perfume he'd crafted just for her.

In these turbulent times, agarwood was worth its weight in gold.
Fortunately, the Evercare Clinic still had a stash of imports from Fuling. This particular ingredient was priceless, and Unfated Tian allowed no one else to touch it.
Agarwood was rich and heavy, clinging to fabric for days. This is a fragrant medicine that could ward off evil and calm the mind.
With careful precision, he scraped a few flakes into a porcelain dish. He hesitated, then added two more.
Unfated Tian always gave Han Xiangxun the best and kept the worst for himself.

Blissful Retreat announced that Madam Han had left to source fresh ingredients, but business would continue as usual.
Meanwhile, in the wilds of Qinghe, several Khitan scouts were found dead. They were poisoned, with no trace of the killer.
Rumor had it their insides had liquefied. Even vultures wouldn't go near them.
No one knew Han Xiangxun was lying wounded at the bottom of a well, recovering from injuries sustained at Still Shore.

The night she woke, she summoned Unfated Tian to meet her there.
"You shouldn't have acted so recklessly."
"You suspect me? I'm a doctor. How could I kill?" He put on an exaggerated look of hurt, though the amusement in his eyes betrayed him.
He knew his acting wouldn't fool her.
"No experience. Got carried away." After she left, Unfated Tian sighed.
If staining his hands with blood kept her safe, so be it.
Eliminating everyone who'd seen her that night was the only way to ensure her peace. Especially when she'd been hurt so badly.

The scent of blended perfumes brought him back to the present. As he finished the new mixture, a faint smile touched his lips.
When Unfated Tian left Han Xiangxun's room, the water clock marked the deepening night.
Soft moonlight spilled into the chamber. Beside her bronze mirror sat a fresh porcelain vase.

zh:
【闵公第四】

【经】
元年，春，王正月。
○齐人救邢。
○夏，六月，辛酉，葬我君庄公。
○秋，八月，公及齐侯盟于落姑。季子来归。
○冬，齐仲孙来。
【传】
元年，春，不书即位，乱故也。
○狄人伐邢。管敬仲言于齐侯曰：“戎狄豺狼，不可厌也。诸夏亲昵，不可弃也。宴安酖毒，不可怀也。诗云：‘岂不怀归，畏此简书。’简书，同恶相恤之谓也。请救邢以从简书。”齐人救邢。
○夏，六月，葬庄公。乱故，是以缓。
○秋，八月，公及齐侯盟于落姑，请复季友也。齐侯许之，使召诸陈，公次于郎以待之。“季子来归”，嘉之也。
○冬，齐仲孙湫来省难。书曰“仲孙”，亦嘉之也。
仲孙归，曰：“不去庆父，鲁难未已。”公曰：“若之何而去之？”对曰：“难不已，将自毙，君其待之。”公曰：“鲁可取乎？”对曰：“不可，犹秉周礼。周礼，所以本也。臣闻之，国将亡，本必先颠，而后枝叶从之。鲁不弃周礼，未可动也。君其务宁鲁难而亲之。亲有礼，因重固，间携贰，覆昏乱，霸王之器也。”
○晋侯作二军，公将上军，大子申生将下军。赵夙御戎，毕万为右，以灭耿、灭霍、灭魏。还，为大子城曲沃，赐赵夙耿，赐毕万魏，以为大夫。
士𫇭曰：“大子不得立矣。分之都城，而位以卿，先为之极，又焉得立？不如逃之，无使罪至。为吴大伯，不亦可乎？犹有令名，与其及也。且谚曰：‘心苟无瑕，何恤乎无家？’天若祚大子，其无晋乎！”
卜偃曰：“毕万之后必大。万，盈数也；魏，大名也。以是始赏，天启之矣。天子曰兆民，诸侯曰万民。今名之大，以从盈数，其必有众。”
初，毕万筮仕于晋，遇屯䷂之比䷇。辛廖占之，曰：“吉。屯固比入，吉孰大焉，其必蕃昌。震为土，车从马，足居之，兄长之，母覆之，众归之，六体不易，合而能固，安而能杀，公侯之卦也。公侯之子孙，必复其始。”

【经】
二年，春，王正月，齐人迁阳。
○夏，五月，乙酉，吉禘于庄公。
○秋，八月，辛丑，公薨。
○九月，夫人姜氏孙于邾。
○公子庆父出奔莒。
○冬，齐高子来盟。
○十有二月，狄入卫。
○郑弃其师。
【传】
二年，春，虢公败犬戎于渭汭。舟之侨曰：“无德而禄，殃也。殃将至矣。”遂奔晋。
○夏，吉禘于庄公，速也。
○初，公傅夺卜𬺈田，公不禁。秋，八月，辛丑，共仲使卜𬺈贼公于武闱。成季以僖公适邾。共仲奔莒，乃入，立之。以赂求共仲于莒，莒人归之。及密，使公子鱼请。不许，哭而往。共仲曰：“奚斯之声也。”乃缢。
闵公，哀姜之娣叔姜之子也，故齐人立之。共仲通于哀姜，哀姜欲立之。闵公之死也，哀姜与知之，故孙于邾。齐人取而杀之于夷，以其尸归，僖公请而葬之。
○成季之将生也，桓公使卜楚丘之父卜之，曰：“男也。其名曰友，在公之右，閒于两社，为公室辅。季氏亡，则鲁不昌。”又筮之，遇大有䷍之乾，䷀曰：“同复于父，敬如君所。”及生，有文在其手曰“友”，遂以命之。
○冬，十二月，狄人伐卫。卫懿公好鹤，鹤有乘轩者。将战，国人受甲者皆曰：“使鹤，鹤实有禄位，余焉能战？”公与石祁子玦，与宁庄子矢，使守，曰：“以此赞国，择利而为之。”与夫人绣衣，曰：“听于二子。”渠孔御戎，子伯为右，黄夷前驱，孔婴齐殿。及狄人战于荧泽，卫师败绩，遂灭卫。卫侯不去其旗，是以甚败。狄人囚史华龙滑与礼孔，以逐卫人。二人曰：“我大史也，实掌其祭。不先，国不可得也。”乃先之。至则告守曰：“不可待也。”夜与国人出。狄入卫，遂从之，又败诸河。
初，惠公之即位也少，齐人使昭伯烝于宣姜，不可，强之，生齐子、戴公、文公、宋桓夫人、许穆夫人。文公为卫之多患也，先适齐。及败，宋桓公逆诸河，宵济。卫之遗民男女七百有三十人，益之以共滕之民为五千人，立戴公以庐于曹。许穆夫人赋载驰。齐侯使公子无亏帅车三百乘、甲士三千人以戍曹。归公乘马，祭服五称，牛、羊、豕、鸡、狗皆三百，与门材。归夫人鱼轩，重锦三十两。
○郑人恶高克，使帅师次于河上，久而弗召。师溃而归，高克奔陈。郑人为之赋清人。
……
en:
【Duke Min, Year 4】

【Classic】
First year, spring, the king's first month.
○ The people of Qi rescued Xing.
○ Summer, sixth month, Xinyou, buried our lord Duke Zhuang.
○ Autumn, eighth month, the Duke made a covenant with the Marquis of Qi at Luogu. Ji Zi returned.
○ Winter, Zhong Sun of Qi came.
【Commentary】
First year, spring, the accession was not recorded, because of the disorder.
○ The Di people attacked Xing. Guan Jingzhong said to the Marquis of Qi: "The Rong and Di are jackals and wolves, insatiable. The various Xia are close kin, not to be abandoned. Idle pleasure is poison, not to be cherished. The Odes say: 'How could we not long to return, but fear this written command.' The written command means mutual aid against common foes. Please rescue Xing to follow the written command." The people of Qi rescued Xing.
○ Summer, sixth month, buried Duke Zhuang. Because of the disorder, it was delayed.
○ Autumn, eighth month, the Duke made a covenant with the Marquis of Qi at Luogu, requesting the return of Ji You. The Marquis of Qi agreed, sending for him from Chen. The Duke waited at Lang for him. "Ji Zi returned," praising him.
○ Winter, Zhong Sun Qiu of Qi came to observe the troubles. The text says "Zhong Sun," also praising him.
Zhong Sun returned and said: "If Qing Fu is not removed, the troubles of Lu will not end." The Duke said: "How can we remove him?" He replied: "If the troubles do not end, he will destroy himself. My lord should wait." The Duke said: "Can Lu be taken?" He replied: "No. They still uphold the Rites of Zhou. The Rites of Zhou are the foundation. I have heard that when a state is about to perish, the foundation must first topple, and then the branches and leaves follow. Lu has not abandoned the Rites of Zhou; it cannot be moved. My lord should strive to pacify Lu's troubles and befriend them. Befriend the ritual, rely on the firm and strong, sow discord among the disaffected, and overthrow the chaotic—these are the tools of a hegemon."
○ The Marquis of Jin created two armies. The Duke led the upper army, and the eldest son, Shen Sheng, led the lower army. Zhao Su drove the war chariot, and Bi Wan served as the right-hand warrior. They extinguished Geng, extinguished Huo, and extinguished Wei. On return, they built a city at Quwo for the eldest son, granted Geng to Zhao Su, and granted Wei to Bi Wan, making them grand officers.
Shi Wei said: "The eldest son will not be established. They divide the capital city for him and place him in the position of a minister. Having first pushed him to the extreme, how can he be established? Better to flee, so that no crime reaches him. To be like Wu Taibo—would that not be acceptable? There would still be a good name, compared to being caught. Moreover, the proverb says: 'If the heart has no flaw, why worry about having no home?' If Heaven blesses the eldest son, will he not be without Jin?"
Bu Yan said: "The descendants of Bi Wan will surely prosper. Wan is a number of fullness; Wei is a great name. To begin rewards with these, Heaven has opened the way. The Son of Heaven is said to have a myriad of people; the feudal lords are said to have ten thousand. Now with a great name following a number of fullness, he is sure to have many followers."
Initially, Bi Wan divined about serving in Jin and encountered the hexagram Zhun (䷂) changing to Bi (䷇). Xin Liao interpreted it, saying: "Auspicious. Zhun is firm, Bi is entering. What auspiciousness is greater? It will surely flourish. Zhen becomes earth; the chariot follows the horse; the feet dwell in it; the elder brother grows it; the mother covers it; the multitude returns to it. The six aspects do not change; combined yet able to be firm, secure yet able to kill—this is the hexagram of a lord. The descendants of a lord will surely restore their beginnings."

【Classic】
Second year, spring, the king's first month, the people of Qi moved Yang.
○ Summer, fifth month, Yiyou, the auspicious di sacrifice was held for Duke Zhuang.
○ Autumn, eighth month, Xinchou, the Duke passed away.
○ Ninth month, Lady Jiang, née Sun, went to Zhu.
○ Prince Qing Fu fled to Ju.
○ Winter, Gao Zi of Qi came to form an alliance.
○ Twelfth month, the Di entered Wei.
○ Zheng abandoned its army.
【Commentary】
Second year, spring, the Duke of Guo defeated the Quan Rong at the bend of the Wei River. Zhou Zhiqiao said: "Without virtue yet receiving emolument is a calamity. The calamity is about to come." Thereupon he fled to Jin.
○ Summer, the auspicious di sacrifice for Duke Zhuang was held, hastened.
○ Initially, the Duke's tutor seized Bu Yi's fields, and the Duke did not prohibit it. Autumn, eighth month, Xinchou, Gong Zhong sent Bu Yi to assassinate the Duke at Wu Wei. Cheng Ji took Duke Xi to Zhu. Gong Zhong fled to Ju, and then they entered and established him. They sought Gong Zhong from Ju with bribes, and the people of Ju returned him. When he reached Mi, he sent Prince Yu to plead. It was not permitted, and he went weeping. Gong Zhong said: "That is the voice of Xisi." Then he hanged himself.
Duke Min was the son of Shu Jiang, the younger sister of Ai Jiang, so the people of Qi established him. Gong Zhong had an affair with Ai Jiang, and Ai Jiang wanted to establish him. When Duke Min died, Ai Jiang knew of it, so she went to Zhu. The people of Qi seized her and killed her at Yi, bringing back her corpse. Duke Xi requested it and buried her.
○ When Cheng Ji was about to be born, Duke Huan had Bu Chuqiu's father divine about it, saying: "It is a male. His name will be You. He will be at the Duke's right, between the two altars, as a support for the ducal house. If the Ji clan perishes, Lu will not prosper." He also divined with yarrow stalks and encountered Da You (䷍) changing to Qian (䷀), saying: "He will return to his father as one, and be revered as his lord is revered." When he was born, there was a pattern on his hand saying "You," so they named him accordingly.
○ Winter, twelfth month, the Di people attacked Wei. Duke Yi of Wei loved cranes, and some cranes rode in carriages. When about to fight, the people of the state who received armor all said: "Let the cranes go! The cranes truly have emoluments and positions. How can we fight?" The Duke gave Shi Qizi a jade ring and Ning Zhuangzi arrows, telling them to guard, saying: "Use these to assist the state, and act according to what is advantageous." He gave his wife embroidered clothes, saying: "Listen to the two men." Qu Kong drove the war chariot, Zi Bo was the right-hand warrior, Huang Yi led the vanguard, and Kong Yingqi brought up the rear. They fought with the Di at Yingze, and the Wei army was defeated, and Wei was extinguished. The Marquis of Wei did not remove his banner, and thus was greatly defeated. The Di imprisoned the historians Hua Long滑 and Li Kong to pursue the people of Wei. The two men said: "We are the grand historians and truly manage the sacrifices. If we do not go first, the state cannot be taken." So they went first. When they arrived, they told the defenders: "You cannot hold out." At night they fled with the people of the state. The Di entered Wei and then pursued them, defeating them again at the river.
Initially, when Duke Hui ascended the throne, he was young. The people of Qi made Zhao Bo commit incest with Xuan Jiang. He refused, but they forced him. She bore Qi Zi, Duke Dai, Duke Wen, Lady of Song Huan, and Lady of Xu Mu. Duke Wen, because of Wei's many troubles, first went to Qi. When they were defeated, Duke Huan of Song met him at the river and crossed at night. The surviving people of Wei, men and women, numbered seven hundred and thirty. Adding the people of Gong and Teng, they became five thousand. They established Duke Dai and lodged at Cao. Lady of Xu Mu composed the poem "Zai Chi." The Marquis of Qi sent Prince Wu Kui leading three hundred chariots and three thousand armored soldiers to guard Cao. He gave the Duke horses, five sets of sacrificial robes, three hundred each of cattle, sheep, pigs, chickens, and dogs, and timber for gates. He gave the Lady a fish-decorated carriage and thirty bolts of double silk.
○ The people of Zheng disliked Gao Ke and made him lead troops stationed by the river. For a long time, he was not summoned back. The army dispersed and returned, and Gao Ke fled to Chen. The people of Zheng composed the poem "Qing Ren" for him.

【告子章句上】

告子曰：性犹杞柳也，义犹杯棬也。以人性为仁义，犹以杞柳为杯棬。
孟子曰：子能顺杞柳之性而以为杯棬乎？将戕贼杞柳而后以为杯棬也？如将戕贼杞柳而以为杯棬，则亦将戕贼人以为仁义与？率天下之人而祸仁义者，必子之言夫！
告子曰：性犹湍水也，决诸东方则东流，决诸西方则西流。人性之无分于善不善也，犹水之无分于东西也。
孟子曰：水信无分于东西，无分于上下乎？人性之善也，犹水之就下也。人无有不善，水无有不下。今夫水，搏而跃之，可使过颡；激而行之，可使在山。是岂水之性哉？其势则然也。人之可使为不善，其性亦犹是也。
告子曰：生之谓性。
孟子曰：生之谓性也，犹白之谓白与？曰：然。
白羽之白也，犹白雪之白；白雪之白，犹白玉之白与？
曰：然。
然则犬之性犹牛之性，牛之性犹人之性与？
告子曰：食色，性也。仁，内也，非外也；义，外也，非内也。
孟子曰：何以谓仁内义外也？
曰：彼长而我长之，非有长于我也，犹彼白而我白之，从其白于外也，故谓之外也。
曰：异于白马之白也，无以异于白人之白也；不识长马之长也，无以异于长人之长与？且谓长者义乎？长之者义乎？
曰：吾弟则爱之，秦人之弟则不爱也，是以我为悦者也，故谓之内。长楚人之长，亦长吾之长，是以长为悦者也，故谓之外也。
曰：耆秦人之炙，无以异于耆吾炙。夫物则亦有然者也，然则耆炙亦有外与？
孟季子问公都子曰：何以谓义内也？
曰：行吾敬，故谓之内也。乡人长于伯兄一岁，则谁敬？
曰：敬兄。酌则谁先？
曰：先酌乡人。所敬在此，所长在彼，果在外，非由内也。

en:
【Gaozi, Part I】

Gaozi said, "Human nature is like the willow tree; righteousness is like cups and bowls. To fashion human nature into benevolence and righteousness is like making cups and bowls from the willow."
Mencius said, "Can you follow the nature of the willow to make cups and bowls? Or must you violate and maim the willow before you can make cups and bowls? If you must violate and maim the willow to make cups and bowls, then must you also violate and maim human nature to achieve benevolence and righteousness? It will be your words that lead all under heaven to bring calamity upon benevolence and righteousness!"
Gaozi said, "Human nature is like swirling water. Open a passage for it to the east, and it will flow east; open a passage to the west, and it will flow west. Human nature does not distinguish between good and not good, just as water does not distinguish between east and west."
Mencius said, "Water indeed does not distinguish between east and west, but does it not distinguish between up and down? The goodness of human nature is like water's tendency to flow downward. There is no human who is not good, just as there is no water that does not flow downward. Now, by striking water and making it leap up, you can cause it to go over your forehead; by damming and channeling it, you can force it to flow uphill. But is this the nature of water? It is the circumstances that make it so. That humans can be made to do what is not good is because their nature is treated in this way."
Gaozi said, "What is inborn is called nature."
Mencius said, "When you say 'what is inborn is called nature,' is it like saying 'white is called white'?"
Gaozi said, "Yes."
Mencius said, "Is the whiteness of a white feather like the whiteness of white snow, and the whiteness of white snow like the whiteness of white jade?"
Gaozi said, "Yes."
Mencius said, "Then is the nature of a dog like the nature of an ox, and the nature of an ox like the nature of a human?"
Gaozi said, "Appetite for food and sex is nature. Benevolence is internal, not external; righteousness is external, not internal."
Mencius said, "Why do you say that benevolence is internal and righteousness is external?"
Gaozi said, "He is old, and I treat him as old. This is not because there is oldness within me, just as something is white and I treat it as white, following its whiteness which is external. Therefore, I call it external."
Mencius said, "There is no difference between the whiteness of a white horse and the whiteness of a white man. But is there no difference between respecting the age of an old horse and respecting the age of an old man? And do you say that righteousness lies in the old man, or in the one who respects the old man?"
Gaozi said, "I love my own younger brother, but I do not love the younger brother of a man of Qin. This is because I take myself as the source of pleasure. Therefore, I call it internal. I respect the elders of Chu just as I respect my own elders. This is because I take their age as the source of pleasure. Therefore, I call it external."
Mencius said, "My enjoyment of the roast meat of a man of Qin is no different from my enjoyment of my own roast meat. Things are also like this. Then, is the enjoyment of roast meat also external?"
Meng Jizi asked Gongduzi, "Why do you say that righteousness is internal?"
Gongduzi said, "I act out my respect; therefore, I call it internal. Suppose a fellow villager is one year older than your elder brother. Whom do you respect?"
Meng Jizi said, "I respect my elder brother."
Gongduzi said, "When pouring wine, whom do you serve first?"
Meng Jizi said, "I serve the fellow villager first."
Gongduzi said, "The one you respect is here, but the one you treat as elder is there. So, it is indeed external, not arising from within."

金缀皇塔，晚来闻钟。有梦堪破，值此夕声。
谁扰了道人清梦？！睡道人惊醒嗔怒，但见落霞如缎，闻钟声迢遥。罢了罢了！扰梦当罚，好景当赏，不如信驴由缰，惬意一回？行至山道，小驴子观前人石刻，似有所感，在崖壁上庄严地摁上了自己的蹄印。道人点头赞之——泥印虽不比石刻久，但也是印。明朝游人见此，如从今朝人驴同游——不问来时，不问归处，只沐晚霞、听钟声……
en:
Gold crowns the imperial pagoda; evening brings the bells. Some dreams deserve to break at such an evening sound.
Who has disturbed the Daoist's sweet dream?! The Sleeping Daoist wakes in a huff, only to see sunset clouds spread like brocade and hear bells tolling far away. Never mind, never mind! The disturber deserves punishment, but such a view deserves admiration. Why not give the donkey free rein and enjoy the moment? Along the mountain path, the little donkey studies inscriptions left by those who came before. Apparently inspired, it solemnly presses its hoofprint onto the cliff. The Daoist nods in approval. A mark in mud will not last like one carved in stone, but a mark it remains. When tomorrow's travelers see it, they may feel as though they are wandering beside man and donkey today, asking neither whence they came nor where they go, only bathing in sunset and listening to bells...

It is a harmless wooden knife, carved by the previous Grandmaster, Raven, its grain still soaked with pine resin.
That year, he used it to exchange for the sharp blade in a girl's hand, as a gift for the grace of not killing.
The wooden knife has no edge and does not rust. Only time has polished it, making it increasingly smooth and warm.
Just like the wooden knife and the iron blade, fundamentally different: one born from trees, longing for sunshine and rain; the other forged from metal and stone, destined to cut through thorns.
Perhaps the moonlight was too beautiful that year, someone knew they were taking separate paths, yet still delusionally wanted to walk a little further with you.

【奔丧第三十四】

奔丧之礼：始闻亲丧，以哭答使者，尽哀；问故，又哭尽哀。遂行，日行百里，不以夜行。唯父母之丧，见星而行，见星而舍。若未得行，则成服而后行。过国至竟，哭尽哀而止。哭辟市朝。望其国竟哭。至于家，入门左，升自西阶，殡东，西面坐，哭尽哀，括发袒，降堂东即位，西乡哭，成踊，袭绖于序东，绞带。反位，拜宾成踊，送宾，反位；有宾后至者，则拜之，成踊、送宾皆如初。众主人兄弟皆出门，出门哭止；阖门，相者告就次。于又哭，括发袒成踊；于三哭，犹括发袒成踊。三日，成服，拜宾、送宾皆如初。
奔丧者非主人，则主人为之拜宾送宾。奔丧者自齐衰以下，入门左中庭北面哭尽哀，免麻于序东，即位袒，与主人哭成踊。于又哭、三哭皆免袒，有宾则主人拜宾、送宾。丈夫妇人之待之也，皆如朝夕哭，位无变也。
奔母之丧，西面哭尽哀，括发袒，降堂东即位，西乡哭，成踊，袭免绖于序东，拜宾、送宾，皆如奔父之礼，于又哭不括发。妇人奔丧，升自东阶，殡东，西面坐，哭尽哀；东髽，即位，与主人拾踊。奔丧者不及殡，先之墓，北面坐，哭尽哀。主人之待之也，即位于墓左，妇人墓右，成踊尽哀括发，东即主人位，绖绞带，哭成踊，拜宾，反位，成踊，相者告事毕。遂冠归，入门左，北面哭尽哀，括发袒成踊，东即位，拜宾成踊。宾出，主人拜送；有宾后至者则拜之成踊；送宾如初。众主人兄弟皆出门，出门哭止，相者告就次。于又哭，括发成踊；于三哭，犹括发成踊。三日成服，于五哭，相者告事毕。为母所以异于父者，壹括发，其余免以终事，他如奔父之礼。
齐衰以下不及殡：先之墓，西面哭尽哀，免麻于东方，即位，与主人哭成踊，袭。有宾则主人拜宾、送宾；宾有后至者，拜之如初。相者告事毕。遂冠归，入门左，北面哭尽哀，免袒成踊，东即位，拜宾成踊，宾出，主人拜送。于又哭，免袒成踊；于三哭，犹免袒成踊。三日成服，于五哭，相者告事毕。

en:
【Mourning Rites, Chapter Thirty-Four】

The rites for mourning: Upon first hearing of a relative's death, one responds to the messenger with weeping, expressing full grief; after inquiring about the circumstances, one weeps again in full grief. Then one sets out, traveling a hundred li per day, not traveling at night. Only for the death of one's father or mother does one travel by starlight and rest by starlight. If one cannot set out immediately, one dons mourning clothes before departing. Upon crossing the border of the state, one weeps in full grief and then stops. The weeping takes place away from markets and courts. Upon sighting the border of one's own state, one weeps. Upon arriving home, one enters through the left side of the gate, ascends by the western steps, and at the east of the bier, sits facing west, weeping in full grief. One then bares one's hair and arms, descends from the hall to take one's position in the east, weeps facing west, and performs the mourning leaps. One then puts on the mourning sash at the east of the hall, along with the hempen belt. Returning to one's position, one receives the guests with mourning leaps, escorts the guests out, and returns to position. If guests arrive later, one receives them, performs mourning leaps, and escorts them out as before. All the chief mourners and brothers go out through the gate, and once outside, the weeping ceases. The gate is closed, and the attendant announces that it is time to retire to the mourning hut. At the second weeping, one bares hair and arms and performs mourning leaps. At the third weeping, one still bares hair and arms and performs mourning leaps. After three days, one dons full mourning clothes and receives and escorts guests as before.
If the one who hastens to the mourning is not the chief mourner, the chief mourner receives and escorts the guests on his behalf. For those hastening to mourning for relatives of the Qi Cui degree or lower, they enter through the left of the gate, stand in the middle of the courtyard facing north, weep in full grief, remove their caps and put on hempen bands at the east of the hall, take their positions with arms bared, and weep with the chief mourner, performing mourning leaps. At the second and third weepings, they all bare their arms with caps removed. If there are guests, the chief mourner receives and escorts them. The men and women who attend to them all do so as at the morning and evening weepings, without changing their positions.
For one hastening to the mourning of one's mother, one weeps facing west in full grief, bares hair and arms, descends from the hall to take position in the east, weeps facing west, performs mourning leaps, then puts on the cap and mourning sash at the east of the hall, receives and escorts guests—all as in the rites for a father's mourning, except that at the second weeping one does not bare one's hair. When a woman hastens to mourning, she ascends by the eastern steps, sits east of the bier facing west, and weeps in full grief. She then binds her hair on the east side, takes her position, and joins the chief mourner in alternating mourning leaps. If one hastening to mourning arrives after the encoffining, one first goes to the grave, sits facing north, and weeps in full grief. The chief mourner's attendant positions him to the left of the grave, with the women to the right. After performing mourning leaps in full grief, one bares one's hair, moves east to the chief mourner's position, puts on the mourning sash and hempen belt, weeps, and performs mourning leaps. One receives the guests, returns to position, and performs mourning leaps. The attendant announces that the rites are complete. One then puts on one's cap and returns home, enters through the left of the gate, weeps facing north in full grief, bares hair and arms, performs mourning leaps, takes position in the east, receives guests with mourning leaps. When the guests depart, the chief mourner escorts them out. If guests arrive later, one receives them with mourning leaps and escorts them out as before. All the chief mourners and brothers go out through the gate, and once outside, the weeping ceases. The attendant announces that it is time to retire to the mourning hut. At the second weeping, one bares hair and performs mourning leaps. At the third weeping, one still bares hair and performs mourning leaps. After three days, one dons full mourning clothes. At the fifth weeping, the attendant announces that the rites are complete. The difference in mourning for one's mother as opposed to one's father is that one bares one's hair only once; for the rest, one keeps the cap removed until the end. All else follows the rites for a father's mourning.
For those mourning relatives of the Qi Cui degree or lower who arrive after the encoffining: one first goes to the grave, weeps facing west in full grief, removes one's cap and puts on hempen bands in the east, takes one's position, weeps with the chief mourner, performs mourning leaps, and then puts on one's clothes. If there are guests, the chief mourner receives and escorts them. If guests arrive later, one receives them as before. The attendant announces that the rites are complete. One then puts on one's cap and returns home, enters through the left of the gate, weeps facing north in full grief, removes one's cap, bares arms, performs mourning leaps, takes position in the east, receives guests with mourning leaps. When the guests depart, the chief mourner escorts them out. At the second weeping, one removes one's cap, bares arms, and performs mourning leaps. At the third weeping, one still removes one's cap, bares arms, and performs mourning leaps. After three days, one dons full mourning clothes. At the fifth weeping, the attendant announces that the rites are complete.

#YPrep Phase#E: #GJun. 26, 2026 - Jul. 3, 2026#E. Guild War enters a new Season. Eligible Guilds are automatically enrolled in the Guild War League and assigned to groups, with up to 200 Guilds per group.

《冶铁之弊》
吾观灌钢之法盛行——以生铁液淋熟铁，反复锻合。然常铁色灰黯，有钢骨不坚之患！
细察其因：
一曰矿杂：铁矿露天堆置，经雨则生红锈，硫土混杂愈甚；
二曰 粒粗：碎矿投炉，风火不透，炭燃未尽而铁已结渣；
三曰 耗巨：欲得精铁，必增燃炭、延火时，民谓‘十斤炭，一斤铁’，痛哉！
今试以 “细矿成球”，非为奇巧，实解三害。
en:
The Flaws of Iron Smelting
I observe that the co-fusion method is prevalent: pouring molten crude iron over wrought iron and forging repeatedly. Yet the iron often appears dull gray, suffering from weak steel structure!
Detailed examination of the causes:
First, Impurities: Iron ore is piled outdoors; rain causes red rust, and sulfur and soil mix in heavily.
Second, Coarse Grains: Crushed ore is thrown into the furnace, but wind and fire cannot penetrate; the charcoal is not fully burnt before the iron forms slag.
Third, Huge Waste: To obtain refined iron, one must increase charcoal and extend firing time. The people say, 'Ten catties of charcoal for one catty of iron.' How painful!
Now I attempt "Fine Ore Pelletizing." It is not for novelty, but to truly solve these three harms.

仓廪无宿储，徭役犹未已。
方惭不耕者，禄食出闾里。

观刈麦
白居易
田家少闲月，五月人倍忙。
夜来南风起，小麦覆陇黄。
妇姑荷箪食，童稚携壶浆。
相随饷田去，丁壮在南冈。
足蒸暑土气，背灼炎天光。
力尽不知热，但惜夏日长。
复有贫妇人，抱子在其旁。
右手秉遗穗，左臂悬敝筐。
听其相顾言，闻者为悲伤。
家田输税尽，拾此充饥肠。
今我何功德，曾不事农桑。
吏禄三百石，岁晏有余粮。
念此私自愧，尽日不能忘。

【渔夫】

渔父歌
李颀
白首何老人，蓑笠蔽其身。
避世长不仕，钓鱼清江滨。
浦沙明濯足，山月静垂纶。
寓宿湍与濑，行歌秋复春。
持竿湘岸竹，爇火芦洲薪。
绿水饭香稻，青荷包紫鳞。
于中还自乐，所欲全吾真。
而笑独醒者，临流多苦辛。

田园乐七首·其三
王维
采菱渡头风急，策杖林西日斜。
杏树坛边渔父，桃花源里人家。

渔歌子
张志和
西塞山前白鹭飞，桃花流水鳜鱼肥。
青箬笠，绿蓑衣，斜风细雨不须归。
en:
[Sentient Beings I]

[Farmer]

Pity the Farmer I
Li Shen
In spring one grain of seed is sown; in autumn thousands more are grown.
No idle fields are seen around; yet farmers starve on barren ground.

Pity the Farmer II
Li Shen
At noon they hoe the grain in heat; their sweat drops on the soil replete.
Who knows the rice upon the plate? Each grain comes from a bitter fate.

Farm Homes on the Wei River
Wang Wei
The slanting sun lights the village below; in narrow lanes, flocks and herds go.
The old man minds his herd boy so dear; leaning on staff, he waits by the door near.
The pheasant calls where wheat is tall; silkworms rest on leaves, in a thrall.
The farmer comes with hoe in hand; they chat friendly, on the land.
I admire this leisure and peace; but sigh and chant "Homeward" with ease.

Song of the Old Farmer
Zhang Ji
The aged farmer lives in mountain's side; he tills a few acres, with crops not wide.
The taxes are high, he can't feed his kin; the grain goes to granaries, turns to dust within.
When winter comes, the plough lies in the room; he calls his son to climb for acorns to consume.
The merchant has pearls worth a hundred gold; on his boat, dogs eat meat, so bold.

Watching the Farm Family
Wei Yingwu
The rain makes flowers fresh and gay; the thunder wakes the earth from clay.
The farmer's rest is short, I say; from now he ploughs and sows each day.
The young men toil in fields so wide; the garden plots are all well-tied.
They come back home at eventide; and lead calves to the stream beside.
They bear their toil and hunger's woe; but rain makes their spirits glow.
The barn has no grain, it is so; the corvee still makes them undergo.
I'm shamed that those who never sow; yet from the village get their own.

Watching the Wheat Harvest
Bai Juyi
Farmers have few months at ease; in May their toil and stress increase.
At night the south wind starts to blow, and wheat turns golden on the row.
Women bring food in baskets light; children carry jugs with might.
They follow to the fields so wide, where strong men work on southern side.
Their feet are steamed by summer soil; their backs are scorched with fiery toil.
Though spent, they feel no heat at all, but fear the long day's curtain fall.
A poor woman is standing near, holding her child so dear.
Her right hand gleans the fallen ear; her left holds a worn basket sere.
I hear her words of grief so deep; all who listen cannot sleep.
Her fields have paid all tax to grain; she picks this to sustain her pain.
What merits have I, who don't plow the land, but enjoy the rice at hand?
My salary is three hundred stones; at year's end surplus fills my bones.
This shames me, I can't hide inside; how can I forget though I tried?

[Fisherman]

Song of the Fisherman
Li Qi
What old white-haired man is here in sight, in straw cloak and hat, by the stream so bright?
He shuns the world and its official ways, by the clear river he fishes all his days.
His feet are washed in the sandy glow, his line is cast in the moonlight low.
He lodges by rapids, roams with a song, through autumn and spring he moves along.
His rod is bamboo from Xiang's shore, his fire from reeds. He needs no more.
The green waves cook his fragrant rice, the lotus wraps his fish of price.
He finds his joy in this his own, and keeps his truth, his heart's alone.
He laughs at those who wake in pain, who by the stream endure much strain.

Seven Rural Songs: III
Wang Wei
At ferry's head I glean caltrops in gale; west of the village, the sun slants pale.
By the apricot altar, a fisher stays; in Peach Blossom Land, a household's days.

Song of Fishery
Zhang Zhihe
Egrets fly before the western hill; peach blooms and fish in stream are seen.
With blue hat and green straw cloak, in wind and rain I am calm and serene.

zh:
开封鬼市深处，藏有一江湖驻地，以地下沟渠水道和地上百坊诸工相连通，奇人异士往来其中。
据门中弟子所传，此门派号曰九流门，乃是江湖第一名门，侠名声于天下，闻者莫不称贤。彼时契丹入汴，门中弟子借地下沟渠地利大败契丹，救民济世，故后皆以此为本署，后虽营运至四海各地，发展为第一门派，亦未忘根本。时至今日，此地街衢洞达，百业兴生，已自成地下小洞天。
吾经此地，得九流门弟子诸多襄助，如此侠义忠胆，敢不钦哉，见贤思齐，不知何以为报，故作斯文存念。
en:
Deep within the labyrinth of Kaifeng's Ghostlight Market lies a secret refuge for jianghu wanderers—a network of underground canals intertwined with bustling streets and workshops above, where extraordinary figures come and go freely. 
According to the disciples, it is known as the Nine Mortal Ways—renowned across the land as the premier and most honorable clan in the jianghu. When the Khitan forces invaded Kaifeng, the disciples, using their intimate knowledge of the subterranean waterways, dealt a crushing blow to the invaders and saved countless lives. Ever since, this sanctuary has remained their heartland. Though their influence has since spread across the realm, growing into the foremost sect of the jianghu, they have never forgotten where they came from. Today, this hidden enclave thrives like a secret world beneath the city—a microcosm where countless trades flourish and a vibrant life pulses quietly beneath the streets. 
As I journeyed through this place, receiving generous aid from many of the Nine Mortal Ways disciples, I was deeply touched by their unwavering spirit of justice and loyalty. Such noble courage deserves the highest respect. I feel obliged to commemorate their legacy in these humble words, though I know no proper way to repay such kindness—only to honor it and strive to walk in their footsteps.

或是因为在她记忆的最初，还没来得及叫做爹娘的男人和女人，在教会她认识更多颜色之前，就急急地把她塞进一个木匣，任她顺水漂流。
她躲在一片黑暗之中，透过木匣上的小孔看见外面闪过流星般的奇异光亮，她一时兴起，用小小的手指堵住这个小洞，又放开。
忽明、忽暗、忽明、忽暗……真是新奇极了。
男人和女人的争执声远去了、如雷鸣般的轰声远去了。
伴着四周潺潺的静谧水声，明与暗，成了她的整个世界。
世界呀，是不是真只有这两道颜色？
直到进了这墨山道，她才发现，树是苍翠的、风是尘白的、不见山的春天山花烂漫，人儿也缤纷。
远处的光明竟然是战火，深处的黑色也可以是一种保护。
好在那时候的她并不知道，二十年后，她能改变许多人命运的颜色。
en:
Before coming here, she once believed the world existed only in black and white.
Perhaps it was because, at the very dawn of her memory, the man and woman she never even got to call "Mother" and "Father" had hurriedly stuffed her into a wooden box. They left her to drift along the river's current before they could teach her to recognize any other hues.
Hiding in the pitch darkness, she peeked through a small hole in the wood, watching strange, meteor-like flashes of light darting outside. On a whim, she used her tiny finger to plug the hole, and then released it.
Light, then dark. Light, then dark... To her, it was endlessly fascinating.
The arguing voices of the man and woman faded away; the thunderous roars faded away.
Accompanied only by the tranquil babbling of the water, light and shadow became her entire world.
Oh, world, do you truly possess only these two colors?
It was not until she entered Mohist Hill that she discovered the trees were a lush verdant green; the wind a dusty white; and the springs of the Hidden Mountain ablaze with blooming wildflowers. People, too, were full of vibrant colors.
She learned that the bright lights in the distance were actually the fires of war, while the deepest darkness could serve as a sanctuary.
Fortunately, the little girl of that time did not yet know that twenty years later, she would be the one to change the colors of countless people's destinies.

During the Tang and Song dynasties, when fisheries flourished, tender perch became the favored choice for this refined delicacy. The art of raw fish reached its golden age then, defined by freshness and flawless knife work.

"Call the boat to dock at the fishing village, perch with fine scales and open mouths await." Caught and served in one breath, sliced into gossamer pieces, it was a taste the ancients considered the height of indulgence.

杠上花常年蹲在横杠旁边。
它不看人做操，不看人练拳，不看人驾车，它只看人上横杠。谁要是翻上去转两圈，它就仰着头，目不转睛地盯着，尾巴尖一颤一颤的。
那个从聊城来的大爷就是被它看兴奋了。大爷说，这猫瞧着我呢，我得给它露一手。然后上了杠，大风火轮转一转，手没攥住，摔下来骨折了。
躺在担架上，大爷还扭头跟杠上花说：看见没？就刚才那几下，记着啊。
杠上花喵了一声，也不知道是在喝彩还是在叹气。
后来没人敢在它面前做危险动作了。摔了真丢人呐，连猫都看着呢。
en:
Barfly squats by the horizontal bar all year round. It does not watch people do calisthenics, nor practice martial arts, nor drive carts. It only watches people get on the horizontal bar. Whenever someone flips up and spins a few times, it tilts its head up, staring intently with the tip of its tail twitching.

A certain elder from Liaocheng got overly excited precisely because of its gaze. The old man said, "This cat is watching me, I have to show it a thing or two." Then he got on the bar, did a giant windmill spin, lost his grip, and fell down, breaking a bone.

Even while lying on the stretcher, the elder turned his head to Barfly and said, "Did you see that? Those moves just now, remember them."

Barfly let out a meow. No one knows if it was cheering or sighing.

After that, no one dared to perform dangerous stunts in front of it anymore. Falling is embarrassing enough as it is, let alone with a cat watching.

zh:
“丁大侠，我认识他，他可厉害了！”——丁璞的前半生仗剑天涯，游历四方；
“那个疯老头？脾气坏得狠，忒顽固！”——可后半生，困于孤岛，俯仰徘徊。
也许人生的一切早就已经注定，可他，从不信命。

梁乾化五年十一月，一个寒冷的冬日。凛冽的风吹过大西北的戈壁滩，发出尖利的啸声。年幼的丁璞在自家屋外发现了一个晕倒的家伙，鲜血在衣甲上流淌，刺得人眼睛生疼。丁璞费了好大力气将他拖进屋子，三日后，那人醒来，大笑着感叹自己命不该绝。他开始教丁璞功夫，却不肯收他为徒，等身上的伤好得差不多了，便留给丁璞一把剑、一壶酒和一本秘籍，潇洒而去。

唐天成二年，江湖上多了一个游侠。人们说他为人张狂执拗，其实却是个好心人，就像一股来自西北的风。风遇山止，船到岸停。丁璞还是遇到了那个让他停下来的人。风停了，停在了开封城。

成亲后不久，有道士说，他这一生六亲缘薄，克父克母，克妻克子，可他对此嗤之以鼻，他不信命。哪怕女儿丁慕儿出生时，妻子难产而亡。他想，他一定，一定要照顾好女儿。丁慕儿满月那天，他在院中的树下埋下一坛女儿红，只待她出嫁时启封喝掉。他教她念书识字，教她家国情怀，还教她功夫——让西坊的臭小子们都不敢欺负她……

人生的选择没有对错，但他还是忍不住问，问自己：后悔吗？如果当年不曾停留，如果她没那么像他，一切会不同吗？没错，丁慕儿太像他了，这不是什么好事。开运四年，契丹入寇，丁慕儿死了，为了救人。他自己也伤了脑子，就这样疯癫了十五年，每日只想着等她回家。

梦总会散，他终归等到了清醒的那一天。那一瞬，百感交集，却只能化为一声叹息。他怀念，愧疚，也气愤。愧疚于自己习武多年，有着极高的武功，却没有保护好女儿；气愤于自己头脑不清醒，荒废了十五年时光，没有给女儿报仇。——不，他不信命。报仇的路，有很多。你看，西北风，刮了起来。
en:
"Great Hero Ding? I know him, he was incredible!" —In his youth, Ding Pu wandered the world with sword in hand.
"That mad old man? Terrible temper, stubborn as a mule!" —But in his later years, he was trapped on an isolated island, pacing restlessly.
Perhaps life's path is predestined, but he's never believed in fate.

In November of the fifth year of the Qianhua era of the Later Liang Dynasty, it was a freezing winter day. A bitter wind howled across the northwest Gobi Desert, slicing through the air. Young Ding Pu found a collapsed man outside his home, blood soaking his armor—a blinding sight. With great effort, he dragged the man inside. Three days later, the stranger woke, laughing that fate had spared him. He taught Ding Pu martial arts but refused to take him as a disciple. When his wounds healed, he left behind a sword, a wine jug, and a martial arts manual, then vanished like the wind.

In the second year of the Tiancheng era of the Tang Dynasty, a new wanderer emerged in the jianghu. They said he was arrogant and stubborn, yet kind-hearted, a gust of northwest wind. Winds stop for mountains, boats halt at shores. But even Ding Pu met the one who made him stay. The wind stilled in Kaifeng City.

Shortly after marrying, a Daoist warned he'd bring misfortune to all kin, parents, wife, and children. He scoffed at the idea. Even when his wife died in childbirth as their daughter Ding Mu'er was born, he vowed to protect the girl with everything he had. On Mu'er's full moon, he buried a jar of Daughter Red wine under the courtyard tree, to be opened on her wedding day. He taught her to read, to love her country, and to wield a sword—so no brat from the west quarter would dare bully her...

There's no right or wrong in life's choices, but he can't help wondering: Do I regret it? If he'd never stayed in Kaifeng, if Mu'er hadn't taken after him so much, would things be different? Yes, Mu'er was too much like him, and that was a curse. In the fourth year of the Kaiyun era, the Khitans invaded, and Mu'er died saving others. The grief drove him mad for fifteen years, daily waiting for her to come home.

Dreams fade eventually. When clarity finally returned, a flood of emotions surged through him, but all he could utter was a sigh. He ached with nostalgia, guilt, and rage. Guilt that his mastery of martial arts hadn't saved his daughter. Rage that madness had stolen fifteen years from him, years he could've spent avenging her. —No, he still didn't believe in fate. There were always paths to vengeance. Look, the northwest wind was rising again.

zh:
采珠，我的妻子，我想给你写这封信，已经有好几年了。但我总不知道怎么和你说，我怕说了，我们的生活就全碎了。
但我更怕，如果我不告诉你，等我死后，没有一个人知道我曾经是谁，我来自哪里。生病之后，我身体一日不如一日，我的恐惧也一天比一天更多……所以我，还是写了这封信，我想把一切都告诉你。
我骗了你，我不是燕北盟的士兵，我是契丹人，我真正的名字，叫枭罗各。那是我们契丹母亲河的名字。

十多年前，我被征入军，离开枭罗各河，来到清河。清河也有河，河边也住着人，和我家乡很像……我不想对这些和我很像的人举起刀，所以我逃走了。
我从清河的地道逃走，却遇到了一个燕北盟的士兵。他只有一个人，但他看我的眼神像狼，我……害怕那样的眼神。
我恳求他，将身上所有的东西掏出来给他，连贴身的牛角项链也拿出来了，那是娘娘做了给我祈福的。但我们都听不懂对方的话，我觉得，自己是要死在这里了。
可没想到，那个人迟疑之后，将刀收回去了。他也没要我的东西，他将项链放回我手里，让我走了。
我逃出地道之后，看见来追捕我的族人，钻进了刚才我来的那条地道。可那个人，恩公，还在里面……
我是个懦夫……我没敢回去，我逃走了，甚至不敢回头看第二眼。他救了我，我却不敢回去帮他。我很懦弱很可恨，是不是？

后来，可汗收兵了，但我回不去了。逃兵是没有资格回去的。
后来，我去收殓了恩公的尸体，我在他身上找到一个帖子，我知道了他叫崔小晋。
再后来，我留在清河，留长发、学汉话，装成一个汉人，遇见了你……之后的事，你都知道了。
原本，我想早点送恩公回他的家乡，但丰禾村有太多太多从前的士兵，我怕他们认出我。等等吧，等麦子熟了吧，等和你成亲吧，等女儿大些吧，我总这么告诉自己，但我始终没动身。如今，我没有几天了，我知道，我等不起了。
我要去送恩公回他的家，等我回来，我便把这封信给你，到时，你想怎样，我都接受。
但我想告诉你，我始终记得，我们在隐月山的枫树下，相遇的那一天。
en:
I've wanted to write this for years but feared the truth would tear us apart. Yet now, I must tell you everything—before it's too late.
I'm Khitan. My real name is Oghuz.
Over ten years ago, as a Khitan soldier sent to Qinghe, I fled through the tunnels, where I met a Northern Vow soldier, and he let me go. Soon, my peers got him in that tunnel, but I couldn't help him. I'm ashamed.
I found my savior's body and learned his name: Cui Xiaojin. I stayed in Qinghe and met you—you know the rest.
I planned to send my savior home sooner but feared recognition. I told myself to wait—for the harvest, our marriage, our daughter—but I never left.
Now, with little time left, I must send him home. When I return, I will give you this letter. Whatever you decide, I will accept.
Still, I want to tell you: I'll always remember the day we met under the maple tree on Moonveil Mountain.

en: When the Five Zang Organs are disharmonious, the Nine Orifices become obstructed. When the Six Fu Organs are disharmonious, stagnation gives rise to abscesses. If evil settles in the Fu Organs, the Yang Meridians fall into disorder. Disordered Yang Meridians cause Qi to stagnate; Qi stagnation leads to Yang excess. If evil settles in the Zang Organs, the Yin Meridians become disrupted. Disrupted Yin Meridians cause blood to stagnate; blood stagnation leads to Yin excess. When Yin Qi becomes too strong, Yang Qi can no longer circulate it, this is called Ge (Blockage). When Yang Qi becomes too strong, Yin Qi can no longer nourish it, this is called Guan (Obstruction). When both Yin and Yang are in excess and can no longer support each other, it is called Guan-Ge (Terminal Collapse). Guan-Ge leads to death before one's natural end.

zh:
朱娘子生了个大胖闺女，红润的脸蛋，敦实的膀子。朱娘子给女儿起了个大气的名，凤英。
别人家的小女娘要学女红，学缫丝。可朱凤英不会。她拈了针线也只会拿着针瞎戳，怎么也不成样子。
朱娘子也不恼，只招呼女儿到厨房来。
“凤英手劲大，帮阿娘揉面。”朱凤英来了精神，一下，两下，小小的女娃和灶台差不多高，却有的是力气。
看着女儿把面揉得又白又松软，朱娘子觉得自己家女儿就是天下最厉害的白案师傅。

路过的邻居看着朱凤英坐在门槛上，总要调笑几句。
那小丫头衣襟沾着白面，捧着大白面馒头，啃得嘴角咧到耳朵。
“这样的小女娘，以后怎么嫁得出去呢！”
而朱娘子总是会提着面杖出来，赶走那些嚼舌的人。

“阿娘，我以后不想嫁人了。”朱凤英啃着新蒸的馍馍，这是她揉得最好的一次。
“那凤英要做什么呢？”朱娘子没有答话，只是掰开了松软的白馍。
“要去做面，做顶好吃的面。蒸馍馍，烙饼子……”朱凤英撇撇嘴，“就是不嫁人了。”
“那要是这样，凤英就是天底下做面最最好吃的小女娘。”
en:
Madam Zhu's daughter was born healthy, with rosy cheeks and strong arms. She gave the girl a name that rang with pride and promise: Fengying.
While other girls learned to stitch and spin silk, Fengying never learned. Give her a needle and she would jab wildly at the cloth a few times, crooked and useless, until even she lost patience.
Madam Zhu never scolded her. She simply waved her daughter into the kitchen.
"Strong hands are wasted on thread," she said. "Come knead the dough for me." Fengying's eyes lit up at once. One push, two pushes—the girl barely reached the stove, but she had plenty of strength.
Under her palms, the dough turned pale and soft. Watching her, Madam Zhu thought: my girl could be the best dough-maker under heaven.

Neighbors passing by liked to tease Fengying as she sat on the doorstep.
Flour dusted her collar. She clutched a huge steamed bun, grinning from ear to ear as she gnawed on it.
"Who would ever marry a girl like that?"
Whenever Madam Zhu heard such words, she would stride out, rolling pin in hand, and send the gossips scattering.

"Mum, I ain't ever getting married,” Fengying mumbled, mouth full of fresh bun. The bun in her hands was the best she had ever made.
Madam Zhu didn't answer right away. She gently pulled apart the warm bun in her hands. "Then what do you want to do?"
"I want to make dough. The best kind there is. Steamed buns, flatbreads..." Fengying scrunched her nose. "Anything, just not marriage."
Madam Zhu laughed, "Then you'll be the finest maker of wheat and flour this world has ever known."

zh:
豆腐脑
若说胡辣汤是早餐的王，那豆腐脑就是后。在中原的早点摊上，这两种早餐主食常常像围棋棋子一样在饭桌上黑白相间星罗棋布，但又难舍难分。有胡辣汤的摊子，豆腐脑如影随形。比起颜色漆黑味道浓烈令人畏惧但又忍不住咽口水的胡辣汤，清白淡雅只有浅浅豆香，光滑柔顺却又一触即碎的豆腐脑带来的是另一种如丝如绸的截然不同的体验。但无论黑汤还是白脑，都好喝，多喝，爱喝，钱袋和胃袋都颇为阔绰的成年人就是可以早餐喝两碗。
en:
2. Tofu Pudding

If hulatang is the king of breakfast, then tofu pudding is his queen. At morning stalls across the Central Plains, the two show up together like black and white stones on a go board, different by nature yet rarely apart. If a stall sells hulatang, tofu pudding is usually right there with it.

Hulatang is dark and bold, the kind that looks almost forbidding but makes your mouth water anyway. Tofu pudding is the opposite: pale, gentle, with just a hint of soybean aroma, silky on the tongue and so tender it falls apart.

Black soup or white pudding, they're both worth drinking. If your wallet and your stomach can handle it, some adults simply order both.

的确，夜里一丁点儿的风吹草动都逃不过它的耳朵。
其实大锣不是从小就这样，这是它的病根。一到夜晚，大锣仿佛回到了十几年前，梦里满街人都在跑，它慌张地从人们腿缝间穿过，躲在树洞里，嗅着呛人的血腥味，一动也不敢动。叮叮当当的刀剑声让它又一次从梦里惊醒。

en:

But Big Gong wasn't always like this. This is his sickness. When night falls, Big Gong seems to return to a decade ago. In his dreams, people run through the streets. He panics, weaving between their legs, hiding in a tree hole, too afraid to move as he smells that choking, bloody scent. The clanging of swords jolts him awake again.
Just then, a wind blows, and leaves rustle down. Big Gong can't help but bark.

zh:
玖儿的鼻子能识良玉。
硬玉软玉、翠玉白玉，只要是上好的玉石，便有股特殊的香气。
玖儿只消嗅一嗅，猫掌一拍，玉工开采！不一会儿篓子便满满当当，玖儿坐在玉石堆上，多么神气！
——哗哗水声打散了小猫的梦。
哪有什么好鼻子、香玉石，只有半条命、空篓子、断绳子。
玖儿在冰冷的溪里漂啊漂，两条腿游不上岸，也沉不了底。
直至一团黑影将它抓着的石头托起，玖儿看见一双如玉的眼睛。
——良玉没有香气，却能温暖小猫的心。
断了两条腿的玖儿，少了一双手的好人。
他们依偎在一块儿，寻玉，寻心。
en:
Jiu'er's nose could sense the finest jade. 
Whether hard jade or soft, emerald green or pure white—every precious stone carried its own subtle fragrance. 
With just a sniff and a gentle tap of her paw, the jade workers would spring into action. Before long, baskets overflowed with treasure, and Jiu'er sat atop the pile, regal and proud. 
But then—the rushing creek shattered the kitten's dream. 
No keen nose, no fragrant jade. Only a half-drowned kitten, an empty basket, a broken rope. 
Jiu'er drifted in the icy water, too weak to swim ashore, too light to sink beneath the surface. 
Until a shadow beneath her lifted the stone she clung to. It met a pair of eyes—smooth and radiant as polished jade. 
Fine jade carries no scent, but it can warm a lonely kitten's heart. 
A kitten missing two legs; a kind soul missing both hands. 
Together, they leaned on one another—searching for jade, searching for hope.

师姐台鉴：
自山门一别，倏忽二载。封龙书院草创以来，蒙天佑护，渐入佳境。今学舍俨然，学子渐丰，内有诸子倾力，外有王兄相护，朝中无异，师姐所虑者今皆安和。
今修此书，实有佳音相报。去岁栾城有乡民负笈来学，躬耕经籍，潜研格致。不意其以朴拙之质，竟参前人未发之奥——于草木染之外，另辟蹊径，以太行红土替之。每观织机轧轧，赤练成章，恍见春雨化生，实令人拊掌称庆。得诸生若此，足慰平生。
忆师姐昔年立志，虽与吾所循异途，然道未尝相悖。今书院新苗初秀，庶几可证当日“知民”之愿。师姐若观此民间智慧绽于庠序，为尔道再添新意，鹤亦不自甚喜。望师姐拨冗一顾，鹤扫榻以待。
en:
To Senior Sister,
Since we parted at the mountain gate, two years have passed in the blink of an eye. Since Dragonbend Academy was first founded, Heaven has been kind, and all has gradually fallen into place. The halls now stand in proper order, the students grow more numerous by the day, those within the academy give their full strength, and Brother Wang lends his protection from without. Nothing has gone amiss at court, and all that once troubled you has now given way to peace.
I write today with glad tidings. Last year, a villager from Luancheng came to study at the academy, carrying his books on his back. He tills the fields and reads the classics, and has quietly devoted himself to the investigation of things. To my surprise, with gifts so plain and unadorned, he has touched upon something those before him had never brought to light. Beyond dyes drawn from plants, he has opened another path entirely, using the red earth of the Taihang in their stead. Whenever I watch the looms clatter and turn, and see lengths of crimson cloth emerge in ordered measure, it seems as though spring itself had quickened them into being. It is enough to make one clap in delight. To have gained a student such as this is comfort enough for a lifetime.
I still remember the resolve you once set your heart upon. Though the path you follow differs from mine, the Dao itself has never run contrary. Now that the first new shoots of the academy have begun to show, perhaps this may serve as proof of that old wish to know the people. If you were to see such wisdom of the common folk flowering within these halls, and find in your own path some new meaning as well, then I should be overjoyed. I only hope you may spare the time to come and see for yourself. I shall make ready and await you.
Yun Xu Rijie

en:
As the old saying goes, "When the birds are gone, the bow is put away." During the Jianlong era, the power of the military waned while the civil officials came to rule, and the affairs of the court shifted like a game of chess.
It was in these turbulent times that Grand Councilor Zhao Pu narrowly escaped an assassin's blade at his own residence, saved at the last moment by the enigmatic wanderer known as the Star Stealer, once a famed vigilante. The jianghu was thrown into uproar, rife with speculation: Who was the assassin? What was the true bond between the Star Stealer and Zhao Pu? What secrets lay hidden beneath the surface?
Some say the legendary Canglang Sword Manual, stolen by the Star Stealer during the battle at Wolf Mountain, is hidden somewhere within Zhao's mansion. Perhaps, if fate allows, future seekers may uncover the truth for themselves.
