zh:
浮光腾跃满亭台，金鳞浮动映楼阁。
昔有黄鲤，争赴龙门，云雨随之，天火烧其尾，乃化龙而去。今有钱塘金鲤，悠游重檐之上，满城高处，无不可见。
鳌山灯壮丽如楼阙，极尽奢华。远观似琉璃灯山，其高数丈，花团锦簇；近看有百戏故事，机关活动；鱼龙噀水，蜿蜒如生。金鲤腾跃其上，悠游楼宇之间，浮光所及，百里烛天。
世人皆贺鱼龙舞，谁念凡鳞未跃时？
en:
Shimmering light leaps across the pavilions; golden scales ripple, reflected upon the towers.
Once, a yellow carp strove to leap through the Dragon Gate; clouds and rain followed it, and heavenly fire scorched its tail, and thus it transformed into a dragon and ascended. Now, the Golden Carp of Qiantang swims at leisure above the layered eaves, seen from every vantage point in the city.
The Aoshan Lantern rises magnificent as a palace tower, extravagant beyond compare. Seen from afar, it resembles a mountain of glass lanterns, towering tens of feet high and adorned with flowers; seen up close, it shows a hundred spectacles and tales, mechanisms set in motion; fish and dragons spout water, winding as though alive. The Golden Carp leaps above it, swimming at leisure between the towers, its shimmering light carrying a hundred miles into the sky.
All the world celebrates the dance of fish and dragon, but who remembers the common fish before it ever learned to leap?

等等最擅长的事便是等人。
不论刮风下雨、电闪雷鸣，每日戌时，等等总会出现在路口，等着主人归来。
可等等不懂，为何自三年前起，它再没等到过主人。
那个人去哪了呢？等等记得主人说过，他在研究飞上天空的办法。也许主人在天上飞呢，一时半会下不来。
于是等等接着等下去。好朋狗喊它玩耍，它不理；戴面具的人类让它挪个地，它不应。等等不想主人回来的那一天，等不到自己柔软的肚皮、毛茸茸的脑袋和高高竖起的耳朵。
那个人也许明天回来，也许永远也不回来。
en:
Waitie's best skill was waiting.
No matter the wind or rain, thunder or lightning, every night at the hour of Xu Hour, Waitie would appear at the crossroads, waiting for his master to return.
But Waitie didn't understand why he hadn't seen his master for three years.
Where did he go? Waitie remembered his master saying he was researching a way to fly into the sky. Perhaps his master was flying up there and couldn't come down for a while.
So Waitie kept waiting. When his dog friends called him to play, he ignored them; when humans in masks told him to move, he didn't respond. Waitie didn't want his master to return one day and find no soft belly, no fuzzy head, and no perked-up ears waiting for him.
That person might return tomorrow, or perhaps never.

zh:
八俊四散后很多年，古乐才重新回到清河。

百草野的风依旧像过去那样吹着，一切看起来和从前一样，但说到底，还是有所不同了。
比如这多年如一日的萋萋芳草下，现今埋着无数曾与他并肩的尸骨。

那场战争有真正的胜利者么？他无法去细想，选择踏上远行之路，或许也是为了避开这种物是人非的悲怆。
他走过很多路，看过很多人，回过头来，突然发现自己还欠他们一曲祭奠的琴音。
于是他回来了，在战场的断壁残垣间，弹起怀思的调子。
弹给当年他未曾参加的最后一战，弹给他未曾见到最后一面的兄弟烈言。

此琴赠故人，此身长相忆。
于是招魂铃发出清脆的响声，遥遥应合。
en:
Many years after the Eight Talents disbanded, Gu Le finally returned to Qinghe.

The wind over Verdant Wilds still blew as it always had. Everything seemed unchanged—yet nothing truly was.
Beneath the same endless sea of grass now lay the bones of those who had once fought beside him.

Had there been any true victors in that war? He couldn't bear to think too deeply. Choosing to embark on a long journey might have been his way of escaping the sorrow of returning to a place where everything was familiar yet everyone was gone.
He had traveled far, seen many faces, but now, looking back, he realized he owed his fallen friends a dirge.
So he returned, and amid the battlefield's ruins, he played a melody of remembrance.
He played for the final battle he had missed, and for Lie Yan, the brother he had never seen again.

This song for departed friends. This life for lasting memory.
And so, the soul bell rang clear, answering from afar.
Huai Tan

zh:
开运三年 十一月廿一
今日又去了叔父的大帐问安，叔父对我依旧冷淡。也是，叔父贵为朝中重臣，每日要见的人那么多，又哪里会把我这个穷困潦倒的远房侄儿放在眼里？
我知道，军营里那些丘八表面对我恭敬，可背地里不知道怎么变着花样儿骂我穷酸。
是，我是扯了叔父的大旗，拉了 “节度使杜重威的远亲侄儿”这张虎皮。可只要这身虎皮还在，这些营里的丘八就合该听我的。
他们凭什么瞧不起我？凭什么背地里作践我——
只有丁笑，只他一个是真心待我的。
我被人暗骂不学无术的时候，是他帮我代写文书。我被人诘问不学无术的时候，是他替我仗义出头。
他……也该真心待我。
他因父兄守城不力，委身为奴时，救他的是我。
他因罪身无处可去，朝不保夕时，给他文书这份生计的，还是我。
丁笑，你不能像那些作践我的人一样。
我拿你当兄弟，你得还我的恩。
en:
21st Day of the Eleventh Month, 946 CE
Today I went once again to Uncle's command tent to pay my respects, and once again he treated me with the same cold indifference. Then again, Uncle is a great minister of the court. So many seek an audience with him each day. Why would he spare a glance for some poor, down-at-heel nephew like me?
I know well enough that the soldiers in camp show me respect only to my face. Behind my back, who knows what names they call me.
Yes, I have borrowed Uncle's name, and wrapped myself in the hide of "Governor Du Chongwei's kinsman." But so long as I still wear that hide, those camp louts should show me some respect.
What right have they to look down on me? What right have they to make sport of me behind my back?
Only Ding Xiao, only he alone, has ever treated me with true sincerity.
When others mocked me for being useless and unlearned, it was he who wrote documents for me. When others pressed me and made a show of my ignorance, it was he who stepped forward on my behalf.
He... he ought to be true to me as well.
When he was reduced to slavery because his father and elder brother failed to hold the city, it was I who saved him.
When, marked by guilt and with nowhere to go, he lived from one day to the next, it was I who gave him clerical work so he could earn his keep.
Ding Xiao, you must not become like those who trample on me.
I have treated you as a brother. You owe me that much.

她们穿的和村里其他小孩一样，吃的和村里其他小孩一样，做的、想的却和其他小孩不一样。
喜儿教孤老头子写自己的名字，球球给生了病的寡妇送糊肚汤。喜儿想成为青州最有学问的教授，球球想开一间不收费用的学堂。

果然，她们都考上了文津馆。蛋羹告诉自己要接受离别，可那一天，蛋羹还是把头埋进了两只前爪里。
糊里糊涂间，蛋羹却被两双温柔的手捞了起来，一路颠簸。在女孩的怀抱里，它见到了一座崖边长桥。
“蛋羹，你爱吃的都带上了，在藏书院里也要听我们的话哦！”
“蛋羹蛋羹，你说，我们会成为很厉害的女史吗？”
她们会发大财，她们会坐马车，她们会游山玩水，她们会学以致用。
en:
The two scribes, Hushou and Yuandeng, usually go by their pen names. But Custard is an old dog; it has seen too much and still remembers the names they had before entering the academy.
Back when it was a stray, two little village girls carried it home. They had plain, humble names: one was Xi'er, and the other was Qiuqiu.
They dressed like all the other village children and ate the same simple food, yet what they did and what they dreamed set them apart.
Xi'er taught lonely old men how to write their own names, while Qiuqiu brought warm porridge to ailing widows. Xi'er dreamed of becoming the most learned scholar in Qingzhou, and Qiuqiu longed to open a school that charged not a single coin.
Custard would curl up between the little girls, listening to their grand ambitions. Deep down, it knew that once they achieved their dreams, they would leave it behind.
Sure enough, both passed the examinations for the Inkbound Order. Custard told itself to accept the parting, but when that day came, it still buried its head between its front paws.
In its daze, two gentle pairs of hands scooped it up into a bumpy journey. Peeking from their embrace, it saw a grand bridge spanning across the cliff.
"Custard, we packed all your favorite treats! Be a good dog in Archive Hall, okay?"
"Custard, oh Custard, do you think we will become renowned scribes one day?"
They will make their fortune, ride in fine carriages, travel mountains and rivers, and put all their learning to good use.

zh:
周威烈王二十三年，夏雨如倾，黄河溢，洛水崩。
三月间，二十七处堤坝告急，三千墨者分赴各地，以肉身负土石填溃口，夜不休睫。然墨者竭力，亦如杯水。
时王册韩、赵、魏，王公云至，典仪煌煌，笙箫沸天。墨子闻之，衣褐履霜，趋入成周，欲谏诸王以救天下。衮衮诸公，只见鼎中牲脂，不问殿外浮尸，更称天道盈虚，非人力可逆，以乱命之罪驱之。墨子悲呼，人命岂不如天命哉？墨子不欲弃，奔走乡野，传百姓疏浚之法，然欲学者竟是寥寥。众人不思自救，反缚童男女沉河，祷苍天以求宽宥，所过数地皆是如此。
是夜，洪渎横流，九州浸溺，亡者千万。墨子泣于废垣，方觉天命为洪，人心至堵，此非诸侯之罪，亦非百姓之罪，乃天之罪。治川壅易，治心壅难。浚川者疏其流，浚心者当破其愚，乃立窥天非命之志。
公孟子劝曰：“天命若锁，镌刻千年。夏商周三代更迭，皆以天命为辞。君欲破此障，恐非一世之功。”
墨子不为所动，曰：“千年之锁，当解以千年之钥。许十年不成，百年无果， 纵千年又有何惧？”
公孟子再劝：“天下不无非命者，敢谔谔者寥寥，何也？君不闻，诸侯以天驭民，百家以天为凭，生民以天为信，君欲与天下为敌耶？”
墨子曰：“诸侯畏天，畏失其鼎；智者畏天，畏失其理；庶人畏天，畏殒其命。然人心至堵，命束于天，岂能畏而退之？昔大禹凿龙门、通九泽，非为己身。今既无人非天，亦当由墨者先行。以义利天下，墨者又岂惜一命哉？”
公孟子拜曰：“君当何为？”
墨子曰：“自今日始，墨者当祛魅飞天，示苍天于众目，纵千载万载，当教天下知晓，雷非天怒、雨非天泣，天命亦不可畏。”
en:
In 403 BCE, the summer rains came down in torrents. The Yellow River overflowed, and the Luo burst its banks.
In the third month, twenty-seven dikes stood on the verge of collapse. Three thousand Mohists were sent out to the breach sites, bearing earth and stone on their backs to fill the gaps, laboring through the night without rest. Yet for all the strength the Mohists spent, it was still no more than a cup of water thrown on a blazing cartload of firewood.
At that time, the king was conferred titles on the Han, Zhao, and Wei marquesses. Lords and nobles gathered in glittering array, the rites resplendent, pipes and drums shaking the heavens. When Mozi heard of it, he put on his coarse robe, stepped out into the frost, and hurried to the Zhou capital, hoping to admonish the rulers and save the world. But those exalted lords saw only the fat of sacrificial beasts within their cauldrons, never the floating corpses beyond the hall. Instead, they spoke of the waxing and waning of Heaven's Dao, of what no human power could resist, and drove him out for disturbing the sacred order. Mozi cried out in grief: Was human life truly worth less than Heaven's decree?
Yet Mozi would not let the matter rest. He went among the villages, teaching the common people how to dredge channels and guide the waters. But those willing to learn were pitifully few. The people did not think to save themselves. Instead, they bound young boys and girls and cast them into the river, praying to Heaven for mercy. Everywhere he went, it was the same.
That night, the flood ran wild, drowning the lands of the Nine Provinces. Millions perished. Mozi wept amid the ruined walls, and at last understood this: if Heaven's decree was the flood, then the hearts of men were the dam. This was not the fault of the feudal lords alone, nor of the common people alone. It was the fault of Heaven. To clear a blocked river is easy. To clear a blocked heart is hard. A river is dredged by opening its course. A heart is dredged by breaking through its ignorance. And so he set his will upon Beholding Heaven and Denying Fate.
Gongmeng Zigao urged him, saying, "If Heaven's decree is a lock, it has stood fast for a thousand years. The rise and fall of Xia, Shang, and Zhou were all explained in its name. If you would break through that barrier, I fear it cannot be done within a single age."
Mozi was unmoved. He said, "A lock of a thousand years must be opened with a key of a thousand years. If ten years fail, if a hundred years bear no fruit, then what is there to fear in a thousand?"
Gongmeng Zigao urged him again. "It is not that there are none beneath Heaven who reject fate, but how few dare say so aloud. Why is that? Have you not heard? The feudal lords use Heaven to rule the people. The hundred schools use Heaven to uphold their teachings. The common people take Heaven as their faith. Would you make yourself the enemy of all under Heaven?"
Mozi said, "The feudal lords fear Heaven because they fear losing their mandate to rule. The learned fear Heaven because they fear losing their principles. The common people fear Heaven because they fear losing their lives. But when men's hearts are blocked and their lives are bound to Heaven, how can one retreat merely because of fear? In ages past, Yu the Great cut through Longmen and opened the Nine Marshes, not for his own sake. Now, since no one else will stand forth to deny Heaven, then the Mohists must go first. If it is for the benefit of the world, what is one life to a Mohist?"
Gongmeng Zigao bowed and asked, "What then will you do?"
Mozi said, "Henceforth, the Mohists shall cast off delusion and ascend to the skies, revealing the heavens to all. Even if it takes a thousand years, ten thousand years, we shall teach the world to know that thunder is not Heaven's wrath, rain is not Heaven's lament, and Heaven's decree is nothing to fear."

zh:
蓬山者，沧海之长岛也。其地沧波万顷，蜃楼隐现，实璇玑枢轴，文脉渊海。绝崖悬星，蛟涛漱玉于足下；穹雾凝霞，琼阁凌虚于云表。天一生水，汇为墨池；地六成书，结作楼阙。圣人像踞其巅，交手而立，携四海文澜；天一楼镇其腑，牙列万卷，藏九州典籍。
阁有思危者，壁列十相，皆怀经世之略，一朝振衣起，咸成济川楫。居有双元者，文武并栖，挥毫可草檄，胸藏九域图。
此地学风朴茂，求道若渴。无论簪缨布衣，但有向学之诚，咸得负笈而入。晨诵诗书，夕研律典，辩史案于竹影之下，析经义于潮汐声中。师者循循，不矜门第；学子孜孜，惟问真知。
馆中诸生，非独雕龙绣虎之才，实乃补天浴日之器。朝论典章以正乾坤，暮筹韬略以安社稷，虽伏案青灯，未尝一日忘激浊扬清、匡扶天下之志也。
赞曰：蓬岛岧岧，文津泱泱。有教无类，斯道大光。观其海涵地负之象，博约并蓄之容，岂非周孔薪传、百代心灯乎？
en:
Penglai is a great island rising from the boundless sea. Its shores stretch across ten thousand acres of surging waves, where mirage towers drift in and out of sight. It is the armillary pivot of the age, the fathomless deep of Cultural Lineage. Sheer cliffs hang among the stars, and dragon-tides wash jade at their feet; vaulting mists gather into rosy clouds, while jade pavilions soar beyond the heavens. From the first waters of creation springs Mo Pool; from the six foundations of earth rise the archive towers. The Sage Statue stands upon the summit, hands clasped, bearing the waves of learning from all four seas. Tianyi Tower anchors its heart, its shelves ranked with ten thousand scrolls, housing the records of all nine provinces.
Within its halls dwell those who contemplate the perils of the age. The Ten Sages line the walls, each bearing statecraft within their hearts; when at last they rise and shake their robes, they become the oars that bear the realm across its rivers. Here too reside the Twin Mavens, who walk the way of both brush and blade. They may draft a proclamation with a stroke, and carry within their breast the map of the Nine Lands.
The spirit of learning here is earnest and deep, and the thirst for the Way unceasing. Whether of noble house or humble cloth, all who come with sincerity of purpose may take up their satchel and enter. In the morning, the Classics are recited; in the evening, the codes of law are studied. History is debated beneath the shadows of bamboo, and the meanings of the scriptures are parsed amid the sound of the tides. Masters guide with patience, making no distinction of birth; students press on with diligence, seeking only truth.
Those who study here are not merely gifted in letters and arts, they are instruments fit to mend the heavens and bathe the sun anew. By day they discourse on statutes to set the world aright; by night they devise stratagems to bring peace to the realm. Though they bend over their desks by lamplight, not a single day passes in which they forget their resolve to purge corruption, uplift virtue, and uphold all under Heaven.
In praise it is said: Penglai rises in majesty, and the Inkbound Order flows vast and deep. Education for All... by this Way, the light shines forth without end. Beholding its capacity to hold seas and bear mountains, to embrace both breadth and refinement... is this not the torch passed down from Confucius, the lamp of the heart burning bright through a hundred generations?
